speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF MINISTER OF LABOUR OF NIGERIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to call to the attention of the house the presence in the diplomatic gallery of the minister of labour of Nigeria, Hon. J. N. Johnson. Mr. Johnson is currently visiting Canada and the United States and recently has been attending the international labour conference in Geneva. I am very pleased to welcome him today. I am sure all hon. members would wish me to express our good wishes to him and to his country, Nigeria, which gained independence within the commonwealth last October, and which is a friend of Canada.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF MINISTER OF LABOUR OF NIGERIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we in the official opposition are happy to join with the Minister of Labour in extending a warm welcome to so distinguished a person as the minister of labour of Nigeria. We not only extend him a warm welcome but in this way we express our admiration for his country.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF MINISTER OF LABOUR OF NIGERIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of this group are pleased to join with the Minister of Labour and the hon. member for Essex East in the sincere and cordial greeting that has been extended to our distinguished visitor. I think the feelings of this group can be best expressed this way. We all take great pride in the commonwealth and its organizations, and are convinced that it can make a great contribution to the peace and prosperity of the world.
One way in which this can be done is by the exchange of men who hold high office such as our distinguished guests here this morning. I know that in Canada we always welcome ministers from other nations and by the mutual exchange of views, opinions and understanding of each other there is given a lead to world peace and happiness. We in this group, are very thankful for the opportunity of adding our words of welcome to our distinguished visitor and hope he will have not only a pleasant but an interesting stay in our country.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-110 to amend the Criminal Code.
He said: It is not easy in dealing with an amending bill of this nature, which covers a variety of subjects under the Criminal Code, to make a second reading speech concerned strictly with the principles of the bill. There are, however, three or four major matters which are covered by this measure, and it may be helpful to hon. members if I outline those parts of the bill which are of the greatest importance and of the greatest interest both to them and to the country.
I should like, therefore, to outline, first of all, the changes which are being made in those provisions of the Criminal Code which deal with criminal sexual psychopaths, a term which we are now changing to "dangerous sexual offenders". Then I will deal with two or three other matters covered by the bill, including the operation of small vessels, habitual criminals generally, and so on.
The first subject, and the one which will be of the widest interest and importance, is that relating to the criminal sexual psychopath.

The problem of the sexual offender is a most complex one. As the house knows, in 1954 a royal commission was appointed under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice McRuer, chief justice of the high court of Ontario, to study the question and make representations with respect to the criminal law relating to criminal sexual psychopaths. This commission presented its report to me in 1958, and that report has been the subject of consideration and study in my department and by the government ever since.
In dealing with the subject it might be helpful if, first of all, I endeavour to outline the problem itself. After that I will describe the amendments which we are placing before the house for its consideration. Finally I shall turn to a difficult question and one which is not covered by the amendments, namely the question of providing for clinics, education and research in this field.
Probably the best way I can give to the house an outline of the scope of the problem is by borrowing from the words of the royal commission itself as they appear at page 59 and following of its report. The commission describes it as follows:
Although sexual offenders cannot be precisely classified, they may be divided into two general groups-those who are a danger to the public and those who are not dangerous but are distinct nuisances. In this inquiry we are primarily concerned with the first class. The legislation we are considering has special application to those who, by reason of some limitation on their power to control their sexual impulses, are likely to be dangerous to society. The principle of preventive detention underlying the law is twofold-segregation to prevent injury to others, and treatment if possible so that the prisoner may ultimately be safely released.
It appears to us that there is no reason why a convicted sexual offender who suffers from no mental disorder impairing his free will and ability to restrain his sexual impulses should not be treated as any other criminal. There always have been and probably always will be in society individuals who seek to fulfil their selfish desires and accomplish their selfish ends through trespass on the legal rights of others.
Again, the royal commission said:
The sexual crimes included in section 661 of the Criminal Code are all crimes affecting the person and are either of a violent or of a corrupting nature which may have devastating effects on the victims, particularly if committed against children.
The amendments which we are proposing to the law on this subject are to a large extent based upon the report and recommendations of the McRuer commission as those recommendations were considered in detail by the commissioners on the uniformity of the law. I should explain that we are not at the present time adopting every one of the recommendations or every part of every recommendation made by the royal commission, but in large part the amendments which I am presenting do proceed from the studies of the royal

commission as amended, or in some cases modified, by the study of the uniformity commissioners.
I should say at once that we do agree entirely with the finding of the McRuer commission that the law as it stands now is not accomplishing its purpose, and, further, we agree that this failure, as the royal commission says, may be due to one or more of three causes; first, the phraseology of the law; second, the lack of proper enforcement of the law; and third, the reluctance of the courts to commit a person to imprisonment for an indeterminate term, especially where there are no arrangements made for custody and treatment of the prisoner apart from those provided for prisoners serving determinate sentences.
There are a number of the amendments which, while arising out of the report of the royal commission, take the form which they have in this bill as a result of the work of the commission on the uniformity of legislation. These are designed to strengthen the provisions of the Criminal Code in relation to this matter and to make them more workable and effective. There is, for instance, the change in the description of the offender from "criminal sexual psychopath" to "dangerous sexual offender". This is based on the report of the royal commission, concurred in by others, that the use of the word "psychopath" is not appropriate because it gives rise to difficulties and misunderstanding between experts in the field on the one hand, particularly when they are called upon to give evidence, and layment, comprising the jury, on the other hand.
It seemed to us to be desirable to adopt a more simple and less technical definition as being less liable to create technical and unnecessary controversy, especially if, as we believe is the case, it is possible to find a phrase which describes the situation we are trying to deal with in non-technical language. With the assistance of the royal commission, we think the words "dangerous sexual offender", based on the reasoning which that commission adopted, do accomplish the purpose of giving a better definition of the type of offender with whom the law is attempting to deal.
Further, we have adopted not only a new terminology in this respect but also a new definition of what constitutes an offence. The present definition of a criminal sexual psychopath is:
A person who, by a course of misconduct in sexual matters has shown a lack of power to control his sexual impulses and who as a result is likely to attack or otherwise inflict injury, pain or evil upon any person.
Criminal Code
The new definition of "dangerous sexual offender" is:
A person who, by his conduct in any sexual matter, has shown a failure to control his sexual impulses and who is likely to cause injury, pain or evil to any person, through failure in the future to control his sexual impulses or is likely to commit a further sexual offence.
I have already dealt with the reasoning behind the change in terminology. As to the change in the definition, the purpose is to make it clear that a court, in an appropriate case, may make a finding that a person is a dangerous sexual offender on the basis of one offence. It was suggested in the evidence before the royal commission that much of the reason why courts have not found, or apparently have not found, the present provisions with regard to a criminal sexual psychopath effective to restrain in custody under treatment those who are guilty of this type of offence is that the law at present makes it necessary to prove a course of conduct probably extending over some years. This has the effect of importing into the law in this field, that which should not be imported and which might be likened to the principle that every dog is entitled to his first bite; whereas it is felt by the commission, and with this line of reasoning we agree, that in dealing with offences that are potentially dangerous and damaging to others, as is the kind of offence embraced in the words "dangerous sexual offender", it should not be necessary to wait until there is a second or subsequent offence, but that the the law itself should define the offense in such terms as to make it possible for the courts, aided by expert medical and psychiatric evidence, to sentence offenders to indeterminate sentence for treatment if, on the basis of that evidence, they come to the conclusion that the offender comes within that definition, whether or not there has been a previous offence.
Another purpose of the change in the definition has been to avoid the extreme difficulty of proving lack of power to control as compared with simply failure to control. After all, what we are concerned with here are the consequences to society of the crime or the offence. Our objective is to remove the offender, thus protecting society on the one hand, and providing treatment for the offender on the other. Therefore it seems immaterial whether the offence is the result of a complete lack of a power to control, requiring technical and very difficult proof, or whether, as is certainly the case whenever this sort of offence is committed, it simply results from failure to control.

Criminal Code
Another purpose of the change in the definition has been to eliminate the implications of coercion contained in the word "inflict". The evidence before the royal commission contained considerable examples of differences of opinion on this point and, indeed, the commission itself referred to a case in the Supreme Court of Canada where the judges of the supreme court themselves were divided on the question of whether or not the words "inflict damage or evil" imported a necessary element of coercion. We felt it was not essential to the determination of the matter to enter into an analysis of whether or not a person, in respect of whom an application has been made to have him declared a dangerous sex offender, may cause the damage in the future by physical coercion or oy mere persuasion and temptation. It does not seem to make much difference what method is resorted to, but it is again the possibility of evil and damage which must be borne in mind here, as well as the elimination of the possibility of that evil or damage. In connection with this particular point, inclusion of the words "or is likely to commit a further sexual offence" was the proposal of the uniformity commissioners.
Again, the amendments relating to dangerous sexual offenders will also clear up the question as to when, in relation to the time of conviction, the application to have a person declared a dangerous sexual offender may be made and the notice of such application must be given. A new provision is included that such an application may be made upon notice thereof being given at any time not later than three months after conviction for the offence giving rise to the application. Under the existing law an application had to be heard before the passing of sentence for the offence giving rise to the application.
It will be noted that we have accepted the argument of the royal commission that the making of an application to have a person declared a dangerous sexual offender should not entitle that person to change his plea if he has already pleaded guilty to the specific offence upon which he is at that moment in court. We have accepted that point of view, but we have gone further. I think in fairness to the house I should point this out, because it should be in the minds of hon. members as they discuss this matter.
We have gone further and provided that the crown may make the application to have a person declared a dangerous sexual offender after he has been convicted, but not more than three months after conviction, and limited in any event, to the time which the offender or convicted person is serving under his sentence. In other words it will
not be possible for the sentence to have expired or have been served in full then for the crown to reach out and make an application based on the previous conviction. However, provided a person is still in custody or, if sentence has been suspended, provided that the sentence is still in effect, and within the limit of three months after conviction, the crown may make application to have that person declared a dangerous sexual offender.
I should like to add a few words on the sentencing of persons adjudged to be dangerous sexual offenders. Under the present law the court, upon adjudging a person to be a criminal sexual psychopath, now to be described as a dangerous sexual offender, must sentence him to a term of imprisonment of not less than two years, and in addition may impose a sentence of preventive detention. The amendment now before the house will eliminate the determinate portion of the sentence because, in our view-and again here we agree with the royal commission-it seems inappropriate to couple a determinate sentence with an indeterminate sentence or a sentence of preventative detention, the main purpose of which is segregation and treatment. I think the reasons for this decision are best explained by the royal commission itself as found at page 65 of its report, which reads as follows:
The mandatory minimum sentence of two years in prison, to be followed by an indeterminate period of preventative detention as required by section 661 C.C., not only eliminates any opportunity of treatment of the prisoner as an out-patient while on suspended sentence, but makes it obligatory that both the determinate and indeterminate sentences be served in a penitentiary. The only qualification is that the prisoner may be confined to a part of a penitentiary set apart for prisoners servicing indeterminate sentences of preventative detention. In theory the sexual offender who comes within this branch of the criminal law is one who at least suffers from some abnormality affecting his sexual impulses. If he does not suffer from any abnormality he does not come within the scheme of the law and should be dealt with as any other convicted person.
Then it continues as follows:
The custody of habitual criminals was discussed in the report of the royal commission investigating the penal system of Canada.
I interpolate here, Mr. Speaker, to point out that their reference is to the Archambault commission which reported in 1939 and not the Fauteux commission, which reported in 1955 or 1956. Then to continue the report:
The recommendations are (1) the sentence of preventative detention should become effective at once and not on the expiration of any other sentence and (2) segregation in an institution away from other offenders.
Then the McRuer commission continues as follows:

-the purpose of the prison (in the case of habitual criminal) is neither punitive nor reformative but primarily segregation from society.
Again the McRuer commission makes this express finding:
All that is said in the Archambault report applies with greater force to the treatment of one who is undergoing preventative detention as a "criminal sexual psychopath", except that segregation should be acompanied by all possible treatment.
These, Mr. Speaker, are the main effects that we hope to attain by the amendments to the law on sexual offenders; that is, the segregation of any person who, as a result of his conduct in any sexual matter, may be determined to be persons likely to commit a sexual offence in the future and thereby liable to cause damage or suffering to any other person. We are concerned with his segregation first, but also his segregation for the best treatment we can devise for him and which is within the limits of our ability to administer in our penal institutions.
This is, however, only the first stage toward the solution of a very complex problem. The reformation, in this case the treatment, of the inmate is only one essential part of any rehabilitation program. The segregation of these offenders, however, will not serve any long term desirable results if the sexual offenders are not treated, so this leads naturally and I think inevitably to a discussion of the establishment of diagnostic and treatment centres, the early detection of cases and the organization of research.
I think it is essential, before I outline the work being done in this field, to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the state of present medical knowledge of this disease. As pointed out by the McRuer royal commission:
The public should understand that it is not possible to speak with assurance about curing the class of offenders we are considering. Many of the medical witnesses who were in a position to speak with great authority took a pessimistic view of the prospects of obtaining satisfactory results from any known form of treatment.
The report went on to state:
Notwithstanding these pessimistic views, we think that a positive attitude toward the problem is of great importance, and a positive attitude demands more than mere custodial care for the prisoners we are discussing. We are convinced that with custodial care must go definite progressive methods of the application of all known helpful means of treatment and the development of new means.
The royal commission recommended that special provisions be made in the penitentiary system for the custody, control and treatment of every sexual offender undergoing preventive detention. In regard to these suggestions I wish to say that the penitentiaries branch is actively engaged on a policy of increased psychiatric attention for all classes of prisoners, including dangerous sexual offenders,
Criminal Code
who appear to be in need of such treatment, and in connection with such policy the penitentiaries branch is studying the best methods of applying such treatment, including the question of how and where dangerous sexual offenders should be confined. In implementing this policy the penitentiaries service is at present restricted by the difficulty of obtaining the services of psychiatrists, and by the limitations of the detention facilities at present available.
It will be remembered that the proportion of dangerous sexual offenders in the prison population is relatively small. No particular question or problem of escape from custody appears to be involved. It will also be remembered that while it is generally recognized that every reasonable attempt should be made to give treatment to those cases willing to receive it and likely to profit from it, psychiatric treatment cannot by its nature be forced upon a prisoner or patient. The McRuer report itself points out that the outlook for successful treatment of those who are not prepared to co-operate in such treatment may be bleak.
The royal commission has recommended that special clinics be set up in co-operation with the courts. In view of the relatively small number of dangerous sexual offenders actually charged and convicted as such, and the high proportion thereof who will be sent to penitentiary in any event; in view also of the fact that the penitentiaries have and are constantly improving the psychiatric services for dangerous sexual offenders, we feel it would be unreasonable and unnecessary duplication at this time to incur the expense of establishing special clinics not part of the penitentiaries system. Furthermore, the establishment of such clinics in what would be really a purely health field is essentially a provincial responsibility.
Although the problem of establishing separate clinics to examine and treat persons who may become dangerous sexual offenders is essentially provincial, the Department of National Health and Welfare is deeply concerned and is approaching the provincial authorities for the purpose of creating interest on their part and discussing with them the manner in which provincial facilities for such diagnosis and treatment outside the penitentiaries system can best be utilized in connection with this problem.
The McRuer commission also suggested a program of education of parents, teachers and all those in charge of young persons, urging them to co-operate with clinics established on the basis, for instance, of the forensic clinic of Toronto so that all known effective measures might be taken to arrest the development in young persons of tendencies toward

Criminal Code
sexual deviation. Again, this is mainly a problem for the provinces to tackle, but the department of my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare is concerned about the problem and is approaching the provincial authorities for the purpose of finding the most efficient and effective solution to this problem. There is indeed urgent need in Canada for research into all aspects of sexual deviation with a view to development of means of correction and prevention. The question of the possible participation by the federal government is under active consideration by my colleague at the present time.
I hope I have succeeded in outlining to the house, in a necessarily brief compass, something of the nature of the problem and of our approach to it, which recognizes that amendments to the law should be based on the principle, first, that a court should be empowered to find a person a dangerous sexual offender on the basis of one offence if the medical evidence indicates that he is a person who is likely to repeat that kind of offence; and second, that the object of the law should be to provide for the segregation of this type of offender for two reasons, on the one hand the protection of society while he is segregated and, on the other hand, the application to him to the greatest degree possible of effective methods of reformation and treatment designed to assist him in curing his deviation so that he may ultimately, in appropriate cases, be released to society without danger to himself or the members of society.
It is, however, always necessary to sound a word of caution in this field as in other related fields. It must be recognized that the dangerous sexual offender is a sick man for whom no assured treatment exists as yet. I should also repeat that, based on the preponderance of medical evidence, it is possible to diagnose "an individual as having a psychopathic personality but we have no specific way of determining what type of anti-social activity he will display". That is actually a quotation taken from the evidence of Dr. Frederick van Nostrand, as it appears in the royal commission report at page 93. So this is a difficult and complex problem about which it is not safe to say with certainty that this or that measure will produce the answers. However, in our view it is a problem with respect to which it is essential to make a beginning, and we trust members of the house will agree that this legislation represents an effective approach to the problem.
I should like to pass now to a discussion of one or two of the other more important amendments found in the bill before the house, the first of them having to do with

habitual criminals generally. The house will appreciate, of course, that the provisions with regard to dangerous sexual offenders, about whom I have up to now been speaking exclusively, are, of course, found in that section of the code dealing with habitual criminals generally, and we have amendments here relating to that subject as well.
One amendment to the provisions relating to habitual criminals parallels the amendment relating to dangerous sexual offenders, in that it permits a notice leading to an application to have a person declared an habitual criminal to be made at any time up to three months following the imposing of the sentence for the offence that gives rise to the application.
Another parallel amendment eliminates the determinate sentence in the case of a person found to be an habitual criminal and sentenced to preventive detention. In the future, when a finding is made that the person concerned is an habitual criminal, the only sentence to be imposed will be an indeterminate sentence to preventive detention. I should point out that in the case of any indeterminate sentence under our new legislation, it is the parole board which determines whether and when the time may have arrived at which it is appropriate to release the person from custody and allow him to spend the balance of his sentence at large in society.
Another amendment which I am sure will be of great interest to the house generally, and perhaps particularly to lawyers, is a provision of the bill which restores the offence of dangerous driving which used to be an offence under the old Criminal Code. At the time of the Criminal Code revision, however, this offence was dropped in favour of the offence of criminal negligence in the operation of a motor vehicle. There is a long history, both in this country and in other countries, of an attempt to formulate an offence under which juries would convict, in appropriate cases, for the reckless or dangerous operation of a motor vehicle which caused death or bodily harm. Juries at one time shied away from convicting persons of manslaughter arising out of death caused by the negligent operation of motor vehicles because of the rather awesome connotation of that word.
This tendency led to the enactment, some years before the Criminal Code revision, of the offence of reckless or dangerous driving, coupled with a provision to the effect that if upon a charge of manslaughter the jury was not satisfied that manslaughter was proved but was satisfied that the other offence was proved, it might convict of that other offence. Apparently juries have tended similarly to

shy away from convicting for criminal negligence in such circumstances. At the present time, the offence of dangerous driving having been removed, it is felt, and widely felt, that there are many cases where persons who have been guilty of criminal negligence in the operation of their motor vehicles are nevertheless escaping with a much milder penalty because of the reluctance of juries to convict of manslaughter or of criminal negligence.
We are accordingly reinstating, at the request of the provinces, the old offence of dangerous driving. We are, however, omitting the word "reckless", because to employ this word seems to have the effect of elevating the offence to the same plane as criminal negligence, thus creating a distinction without a difference which would make it very difficult to charge juries.
There is also an amendment making the offence of driving a motor vehicle while the person is disqualified or prohibited from doing so by reason of the suspension of his licence by the court or a motor vehicle registrar, an offence punishable upon indictment as well as upon summary conviction, which is now the case, and imposing a more severe penalty when the charge is proceeded with by way of indictment.
Another provision in this bill, which I am sure will be of great interest, has the effect of transferring to the Criminal Code a number of provisions now found in the small vessels regulations. For some years there have been in the small vessel regulations, enacted under the Canada Shipping Act, a series of sections paralleling those in the Criminal Code relating to abuses in connection with motor vehicles; namely operating a vessel or towed object, such as water skis, dangerously or while the ability of the operator is impaired by alcohol or a drug, or leaving the scene of an accident with intent to escape liability; and providing that the court, when convicting for such offences, may make an order prohibiting the person convicted from operating a vessel for a stated period.
Of late years, as all hon. members know, the number of small pleasure craft on the domestic and territorial waters of Canada has greatly increased and a great many accidents, in some cases fatal, have recently been caused by the careless operation of such craft. We consider that this problem has now become so acute that measures to deal with it should be in the Criminal Code. While those provisions were to be found only in the regulations under the Canada Shipping Act, they have tended to be regarded as rather special provisions of interest chiefly to the Department of Transport, or at any rate to the federal government alone; by including them in the code we hope they will be recognized as an ordinary part of the criminal law made
Criminal Code
necessary by new conditions and will be enforced by provincial authorities in the ordinary course of Criminal Code enforcement.
There are, as will be appreciated, a number of other amendments in the bill. I think I have picked out the amendments of greatest interest and concern, at least I have endeavoured to do so, in an effort to be as helpful as possible to the house in outlining the thinking of the government which has given rise to this amending bill.
I should say also, Mr. Speaker, that it is my view, and my colleagues have agreed with me in this, that generally speaking amendments to the Criminal Code should not be made every year. It seems to me that, as nearly as possible, the criminal law should be certain. It is not desirable, then, that changes should be made too rapidly or too frequently. Every change necessarily imports the necessity for building up new jurisprudence on the change and may, in ways quite unforeseen, have the result of confusing settled jurisprudence. We do not think it is desirable in the field of criminal law that this should take place, at least with frequency.
I wish to emphasize that this does not indicate that we will refuse to consider necessary changes or to discuss with anyone the necessity for a change. It is merely that we feel, in general, changes to the Criminal Code should be made as a matter of real deliberation, and as infrequently as will meet the necessities of the case. This is one reason there is a fairly substantial bill this year. There was no Criminal Code amending bill last year.
Of course if a case in the courts or a situation in the country arises, indicating an emergency and indicating urgent necessity for an amendment, we would not then be so foolish as to say we do not believe in amending the Criminal Code every year and therefore we will not introduce such an amendment. The necessary amendment would be recommended to the house at once where there was any real necessity for it. In general, however, our thought is that there should be a Criminal Code amending bill only every two or three years. This is one of the reasons for the size of the present bill.

Mr. Speaker, in introducing the amendments to the Criminal Code the minister prefaced his remarks with an apologia to the effect that it was difficult to speak to matters of principle in connection with this bill because its 45 amending provisions deal with so many different aspects of the criminal law. I hope the minister and the house, in listening to my remarks, will bear in mind the fact that if it is difficult for the minister, who has had the bill in charge for some time, it is even

Criminal Code
more difficult for the opposition members who only saw the bill for the first time this morning. There are a number of remarks which I should like to make, Mr. Speaker, concerning these provisions, and perhaps I might do so in reverse order to those touched upon by the minister.
In so far as the small vessels regulations are concerned which have been incorporated into Bill No. C-110, as the minister stated those provisions have been in the law and have been the responsibility of the Department of Transport for some time. The necessity for enforcing them, therefore, has lain with the R.C.M. Police. As the minister indicated, this responsibility now passes to the provincial police of those provinces which have provincial policing authorities.
Speaking generally to the principle, I suggest that they are good provisions. They have been in the Canada Shipping Act for some time. However, care must be taken in enacting legislation not to enact it purely because it appears to meet a need or because it appears to be a good thing. This should not be a kind of "busy" work just to justify a department. Laws enacted by this parliament should be those which not only meet a need but which are enforceable.
It is well known, I think to most hon. members of the house that the R.C.M. Police have had difficulty in trying to enforce these regulations. Their numbers are comparatively small. The problem itself is acutely difficult because of the thousands and thousands of small lakes and hidden waterways within Canada. If the R.C.M.P. who have been dealing with this matter for some time are incapable of handling the matter, it is highly unlikely that the provincial police forces, which call annually for more personnel and which are annually running well behind the necessary personnel even to police the highways, will be able to provide sufficient personnel to police the waterways. When I think of the many lakes, even in the area surrounding Ottawa to which hon. members have resort on Sundays while the house is in session, and the number of boats such as those I saw yesterday speeding through the lakes with no member of a provincial police force anywhere for miles around, it seems to me that we must be careful not to congratulate the minister or the government, or not to be content that by the mere proposal and passage of a section in the Criminal Code or under the Department of Transport regulations we have thereby solved the problem. The mere fact that we have enacted legislation, unless we have sufficient policing authority to enforce it, is useless verbiage.
I would hope that the minister would be able to advise us, either now or later, of

some provisions which may be made for special policing authorities. It may be that in his discussions with the provinces, which I presume were held prior to the introduction of these sections into the Criminal Code, some arrangement has been made with the provincial attorneys general to provide more policing authorities, particularly as we are now into the summer season and there are thousands more small boats in use each year. I think this is a good provision if it is enforceable. If it is not enforceable, then it only weakens the criminal law to include it.
With respect to the provisions in Bill No. C-110 dealing with driving while under suspension, may I say that it has been my experience and, I think, that of most of the hon. members of the house who are of the legal fraternity, that the public generally does not view this offence as serious. By now making it capable of being prosecuted as an indictable offence with a vastly more serious penalty, it may be that the public generally will accept this as a more serious matter and will be deterred from driving while under suspension. To carry the same provision into the operation of a small vessel only points up, I think, how difficult it is to police those provisions with respect to small vessels. I have been told at various times by members of policing authorities that they would estimate that there are 10 drivers on the highway driving without licences or with licences under suspension for every one who is caught in the process of doing so. I imagine that these figures would be vastly greater if one were to consider those operating small vessels with licences under suspension. Again I repeat that the mere enactment of legislation is insufficient and weakens the criminal law unless there are enough provisions for enforcing it.
As to the amendment to replace in the Criminal Code the offence of dangerous driving, may I say this. As the minister knows and has mentioned, this has a long history of difficulty in the criminal law. When the act was amended in 1955 it was dropped for a particular purpose, as it was felt that there would be convictions under what was at one time motor manslaughter but is now criminal negligence in the use of a motor vehicle. As a matter of practice, as the minister has said, juries do not convict because there has been telegraphed to them the fact that this is the old motor manslaughter provision. There appears to be a feeling in the community that manslaughter is not the proper name, that it does not carry the proper intent, when connected with a motor vehicle. The public generally seems to feel that that is an almost deliberate sort of killing.

Accordingly, it may well be that there are many individuals who have been guilty of driving in a manner which has caused grievous bodily harm, in some cases death, and in other cases considerable property damage, who ought to have been convicted of some offence and to have suffered a monetary penalty or a penalty by incarceration, but who have not convicted by virtue of the fact that this section was not in the code. Its reinstitution I would suppose has been suggested by provincial authorities and would be greeted by them with some pleasure. It cannot be said, however, that defence counsel would greet it with the same pleasure.
As to the provisions respecting habitual criminals, may I say that this is perhaps the greatest single deterrent which is in our criminal law. In my experience with habitual criminals or those who characterize themselves as professional thieves or professional robbers-and there are, shockingly enough, in Canada those who pride themselves on this title-they are all afraid of what they call "the bitch". As they collect a record of convictions they come terrifyingly close to the point where a crown attorney may lay this charge. Within the brief span of my 11 years in practice, most of which has been in criminal law, I found that nothing deterred or frightened a professional criminal with a record as much as the possibility of a charge of being an habitual criminal.
I think the provision which is being instituted by this amendment is one which must be approached with caution. Although it strikes terror into the hearts of criminals-* and that is what we want for one who is an habitual criminal-we have to bear in mind that this is not an offence in the usual understanding of that term. It is a condition; what the court is asked to find is that a person is in such a condition that in fact he cannot be reclaimed to society, as indicated by a long history of convictions for varying criminal offences. Because I think we recognize that all individuals in society may commit crimes, no matter how heinous, and may be reformed, we must be careful in the use of this charge, or this application to have a person so found. Notwithstanding a long and vicious record, it is possible that some intervening act may happen to make them reclaim themselves.
The fact that now it will not be necessary to serve this notice and have the same jury which convicted an individual of a criminal offence deal with the application to find him as an habitual criminal works in two ways, or can possibly do so. One of these can certainly be as a deterrent to an individual who has been charged with an offence and has been convicted but who, in the time after conviction and prior to the expiration of three
Criminal Code
months, feels that he can rehabilitate himself; then shortly before the expiry of the three months he finds that the crown authorities have laid this charge against him.
I would call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker, if I may do so.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, before the luncheon adjournment I was discussing some of the provisions of this bill with which the minister had dealt in the latter part of his statement. Before leaving that part of it I might make one other suggestion. Many people who have dealt with the question of habitual criminals are of the opinion that this provision is not used sufficiently. I do not have the statistics, nor has the minister placed them before us, of the number of habitual criminal convictions which have been obtained in Canada since this provision was put into the Criminal Code. However, I have heard it discussed at various times by those involved in the administration of justice, and I have heard the suggestion that there should be a definite time laid down after which there should be no discretion in the crown attorney. In other words, on the third or fourth criminal conviction there must be an application made to the court to find the individual concerned to be one who is an habitual criminal. I wonder if the minister, when he discusses this matter later, would comment on whether this suggestion has been considered by the department and what the rationale of the department was in deciding not to include it.
I should like to pass on to the clauses of the amending bill which deal with those who until now have been called criminal sexual psychopaths. My experience of this matter has been in discussing it with a member of the royal commission which was chaired by Chief Justice McRuer, a person of whom in my riding and county we are very proud, in particular those of my sex. I refer to Her Honour Judge Kinnear of the county court of Ontario, who was the first woman appointed by the previous administration to this level of the judiciary and who still remains senior in this post throughout the commonwealth and the empire.
She was a member of the commission which dealt with the difficult question of criminal sexual psychopaths, and over the years I have had the benefit of discussing this question with her. Chief Justice McRuer, who

Criminal Code
chaired the commission, has the widest practical criminal experience in Ontario, and the recommendations included in the report of that commission are lucid and humane. It is with some regret that I notice this bill does not include a provision for research and clinical facilities such as were recommended by the royal commission. I understand from the statement of the minister that consideration of this matter has not ceased, and that in the future it may be possible to make provision for more facilities, but the intention now is that anyone convicted as a dangerous sexual offender under these amendments will be required to go to a penitentiary.
The royal commission report is very definite on the point that this is of little real assistance and that there are two factors which keep many such offenders from becoming cured or rehabilitated. One is that most sexual offenders do not choose to be rehabilitated. This is, in many sexual offences this is a way of life which they have adopted and which they choose to pursue. The other is one which the minister mentioned, that so far medical science has discovered no real cure for one who does not wish to be changed.
Certainly the change of style from "criminal sexual psychopath" to the style in the present bill of "dangerous sexual offender" is good. In particular I think it might be interesting for the house to note that in the evidence of the psychiatrists who were called before the McRuer commission the first quotation was a remark of Dr. B. H. McNeill of the Ontario department of health, who said "I once heard a psychopath defined by a psychiatrist in the same way as he said someone defined a hippopotamus; he could not define it but he knew one when he saw it". This points up the fact that psychiatry has not as yet been able to define or pinpoint what it is that is wrong with these people and thus take a first step toward their cure. Certainly within the experience of certain criminals whom I have defended there is in the penitentiary system wide scope for abnormality of sexual experience which this bill will not cure, because even though these people are segregated within the penitentiary system there will still be opportunity for this abnormality to continue without any real treatment and without at present any real hope that they may be cured.
Many suggestions were gone into by the commission when they dealt with this subject. While it is a knotty and difficult one, partly legal and partly medical, it is encouraging, I think, for hon. members of the house to remember that the numbers involved are very small; that most of those who are guilty of sexual offences are only

what are known as common nuisances and that the really dangerous criminal offenders are very much in the minority. Thus we are legislating with respect to only a few people, although those few people are capable of wreaking great damage on other people and particularly on very young children.
We should be careful, however, when dealing with any offence which may bring about a term of preventive detention that we do not infringe on the rights of all under the bill of rights or under the natural rights of people in this country. We have to be satisfied first that there is, in fact, a condition there which cannot be cured in our present state of medical knowledge. Second, even if a cure is available it may not be accepted by the individual concerned, since it is necessary to have sympathy and empathy between the psychiatrist and his patient. Third, we must consider whether simply removing these people from society is sufficient.
We hear in this field very little discussion of points which arise in the consideration of murder, such as what is a deterrent, what is the retribution of society and what is the rehabilitation of the criminal. We admit we cannot rehabilitate these people. We deny, I think generally, that what we are asking for is retribution. I would ask the minister upon what philosophy he has based the provisions he now places before the house in order to remove these people from society for a more or less permanent period which may be the rest of their lives.
The provisions of the clause dealing with dangerous sexual offenders are generally noncontentious, inasmuch as they were largely recommended by the McRuer commission. That commission, however, did not stop with these recommendations. Ten of the 20 or more points made dealt with questions beyond the Criminal Code, in particular with the urgent need in Canada for research into all aspects of this problem and the need to develop a means of correction and prevention. The commission pointed out that the psychopathic sexual offender is no different from any other offender, that he is in effect an ill man, as the minister also pointed out. The commission drew the conclusion that our only course is simply to segregate these people from society; that we should not cover this with a feeling that we are doing something for these people who are ill, but that we must recognize that at this point there is little we can do for them even if they were willing to co-operate.
All we can do is merely remove the festering canker from society and place where it cannot be communicated. This, of course, is communicable if left in society because the

Criminal Code
aberrations of some individuals cause them to bring in younger and younger people, and it spreads. It may, therefore, be justifiable simply to remove them from society. However, we should not pride ourselves that because we are taking them out of society we are doing this for their good. This removing of offenders from society is nothing but punitive legislation for society's good.
The provisions of the bill are similar to those which apply to habitual criminals, in that this offence may be charged within a period following conviction. I would again caution the minister, as I did before the luncheon break, about the obvious dangers of this. Once having faced trial on a sexual offence and having been found guilty, any time within the following three months an individual may be faced with a further charge and prosecuted.
There are a number of things which were recommended by the royal commission which the government has not yet seen fit to adopt. I understand from the minister's statement this morning that unless something arises of an emergent nature it is unlikely that we shall see another amendment to the Criminal Code during the life of this parliament. The hon. gentleman indicated clearly that be believed amendments should only be introduced every second or third year. While I agree that it is very necessary to have a degree of certainty in criminal law in order that a body of jurisprudence may be built up and in order that there should be time to see how the legislation operates, I decry the rigidity of saying that unless there is something of an emergent nature we shall not amend it from time to time.
It may be that it will take more than three years for the effects of this legislation to become known. Of course if we do not pass it we shall never find out what its effects might have been. However, it may be that within a year after its passage we find that further amendments need to be brought forward, amendments more in conformity with the report of the royal commission, particularly in connection with whatever assistance may be given sexual offenders in providing research and clinical facilities and, especially, by providing a separate place in which to segregate them where they would receive treatment, rather than receiving treatment in other parts of the penitentiary where they are at liberty to move among other prisoners.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Would the hon. lady not agree that a provision of that kind would not necessarily be made by way of amendment to the Criminal Code, but more likely would be
made by other legislation, possibly under the Penitentiaries Act or within the field of responsibility of the Minister of National Health and Welfare?

I do agree with the minister that it is likely this would come in elsewhere. There were, of course, other recommendations respecting amendments to the evidence act and amendments to the Penitentiaries Act. I have not seen these on the order paper, and it may be that the minister will be bringing those in shortly.
If I may sum up, Mr. Speaker, we on this side approve in general, I would say, the adoption of the recommendations of the commission. These were reported to the Minister of Justice in 1958, and for three years now they have been available to the public, to psychiatrists and to those law officers who would be interested. The minister announced that a study had been made by the commission on the conformity of legislation. The hon. gentleman said that having had the benefit of its report he had modified the report of the royal commission, adopting some of its recommendations but not others.
We are in sympathy with stern treatment for those who as ravening monsters prey sexually on small children. We are also in sympathy with those who are ill, who have committed these offences and who wish to stop being deviates and avoid getting into such trouble again. We are in sympathy, I would say, with the principle of preventive detention, because this permits flexibility in that each person convicted of an offence may, as the individual reaches the point where he is no longer a danger, be freed without the rigidity which is necessarily so often a part of the criminal law.
We shall have remarks to make at the committee stage not only on these clauses but on other clauses with which I dealt prior to the noon adjournment. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, it is difficult to deal with the principles involved in a bill which covers so many subjects, linked only because they come under the umbrella of the Criminal Code. However, in principle the amendments are largely ones of which we approve although, as I stated before, we reserve our right at the committee stage to complain about certain of them. It may well be, Mr. Speaker, that the minister will find certain amendments being put forward, either with respect to the material now dealt with or additional material, since we have been warned in effect that we cannot expect other amendments to the Criminal Code for some years.

Criminal Code

Mr. Speaker, this bill contains several principles, as the minister has indicated, and I should like to say a few words about the main ones.
I should like to refer in general terms to amendments to the Criminal Code, and draw to the attention of hon. members the progressive manner in which the Minister of Justice has brought before this house problems which have been seriously troubling many people of this country. During this session we have considered the most serious problem regarding the question of capital punishment, in respect to which there were many satisfactory proposals made and accepted by this house. The Minister of Justice has also brought forward a bill dealing with narcotics control and treatment of offenders. This involves another serious problem which has concerned many people in this country.
I suggest there are two main principles involved in the bill presently before us. The first deals with the provision of a stern code of regulations to prevent individuals from turning our waterways into speed zones and death traps when they should be used for the pleasure of individuals. The second principle embodies an effective method, which the minister has proposed, to deal with dangerous sexual offenders. There is of course also the provision having reference to the reinstatement of the dangerous driving section of the Criminal Code, to which I should like to refer briefly later on in my remarks.
In relation to the dangerous operation of vessels on our waterways, I suggest this has been a problem of serious concern to individuals throughout Canada and particularly to those resident in my area of the country, which has a very important tourist industry. For many years the waters of Canada, and particularly the inland waters, have been used for pleasure by individuals on fishing holidays, or just for travel from one place to another, as well as by those who wanted to take a vacation away from crowds of people.
With the advent of high powered engines and lighter and smaller craft, dangers on inland waters have become very great. Not so many years ago people were satisfied to have boats equipped with 2J horsepower motors, and to cruise slowly along the water enjoying themselves. Today there exist many high powered engines mounted on very light craft, which in itself creates a danger, used by individuals for travelling around our inland waters at high and very dangerous rates of speed. I do not suggest it is always young people who operate these boats in that fashion. It is very easy to blame this wild speeding on teen-agers, but I suggest that on many

occasions adults are guilty of this same dangerous practice. It seems that when an individual puts a high powered motor on a small craft he likes to feel the power behind him and takes the attitude that while travelling on open water there is not likely to be anyone else in the area.
The minister has pointed out, in introducing this bill, that there are small vessels regulations in existence under the shipping act, but that the main problem involved has been one of enforcement. Operators of these motor boats apparently have not been impressed by the existence of these regulations. While they do exist, I suggest, like the provision of library book fines, they are not taken seriously. Perhaps the reason for this is that these regulations come under the Department of Transport. I suggest that by placing these regulations under the Criminal Code it will be drawn to the attention of the public, particularly operators of these small craft, that infractions of these regulations are considered to be serious matters, to be seriously dealt with.
The Department of Transport has issued a small booklet entitled "Safety Afloat" with wide distribution among pleasure craft operators, but it has not been receiving the attention it deserves. In appendix 4 of that booklet appears a list of offences and penalties under the small vessels regulations. I feel that this has been a polite reminder to operators of small craft of the existence of the regulations. However, in view of the apparent lack of concern and attention, the time has now arrived when action must be taken in a manner which is not merely polite but also effective in preventing the continued infraction of these regulations by the operators of small boats on our public waters.
I suggest the new amendment to the Criminal Code covering the regulations in respect of the operation of small vessels will constitute a clear indication to those operators that this situation is considered serious. I believe there will be no reason, following proper publicity given to this change in the regulations, for individuals to consider them only as polite reminders.
I suggest one other problem which has resulted from the fact that the regulations were under the shipping act has involved their enforcement. There has been some difficulty in persuading municipal and provincial police forces that these regulations in respect of inland waters under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport should be enforced by them. Those forces have taken the attitude that the enforcement of these regulations was a matter of concern

to the mounted police force only. This attitude exists particularly in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, which are policed in the main by provincial police forces. I suggest, therefore, that there has been some gap in respect to the responsibility of enforcing these regulations on our public waters.
While it is true that the provincial police have on several occasions, certainly on the Muskoka lakes, established patrols similar to those established by the mounted police, I feel it is understandable to all hon. members that it is impossible for these patrols to enforce these regulations on all the lakes and streams throughout these districts. I suggest that the inclusion of these provisions in the Criminal Code will make clear that the responsibility for enforcing the regulations lies to a great extent upon the provincial and municipal police forces, and thereby will remove a great deal of doubt which I suggest has existed in the past in this regard.
I feel that many of these provincial and municipal forces have considered that the mounted police, particularly in Quebec and Ontario, are a specialized force designed to carry out the enforcement of federal laws, and that lack of effective enforcement of those regulations within the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport has resulted from the lack of sufficient personnel in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police force. For the reasons I have stated, I am very pleased that the Minister of Justice has seen fit to bring these regulations under the Criminal Code in respect to navigation on the waters of this country.
The second subject which I should like to deal with has reference to dangerous sexual offenders. I feel that the existence of these dangerous sexual offenders in our communities has been perhaps the greatest source of worry to parents in this country, and that the inadequacy of the law in respect to them has been obvious for quite a number of years. We all know that a royal commission was set up under the chairmanship of Chief Justice McRuer of Ontario, which reported to the Minister of Justice on March 21, 1958. That commission found that in addition to an inadequacy in law there was an inadequacy in definition as to the type of individual who ought to be dealt with as a criminal sexual offender. I suggest that the amendment now introduced by the Minister of Justice in this connection contains great advances in this matter. Occasionally it is said jokingly, if you cannot do anything about a certain subject, appoint a royal commission. But here is an example, among many others, of where a royal commission has made a very thorough review of a difficult subject and has brought forward good
Criminal Code
recommendations. I commend the Minister of Justice for accepting them almost without hesitation and certainly without any alteration of the main principles of the report.
In the report the commission came to a number of conclusions and made a number of recommendations with regard to sexual offenders. As found in the summary of conclusions on page 123, they conclude first that the use of the word "psychopath" as applied to the class of sexual offenders coming within the terms of reference is undesirable. During the course of the commission's hearings, many of those who appeared before it tried to define what a psychopath was and it was found that to a large extent it was undefinable. To a considerable extent the definition depended entirely on the evidence of one psychiatrist or another and, as we know, psychiatry has not developed to the point of absoluteness where there can be any sort of agreement.
I think the recommendations made by the royal commission and accepted by the minister with regard to defining the type of person and the offence constitute a much better criterion than trying to define a criminal sexual psychopath, and in that regard the first recommendation of the McRuer commission, as found on page 127 of its report, was adopted. The McRuer commission recommended the use of the words "dangerous sexual offender" and defined them in almost the precise terms that are found in the bill now before us.
The commission also recommended that section 661 of the Criminal Code should not be extended to cover any offences not named therein. An examination of the bill indicates that this recommendation has been carried out and that the same offences now listed in the Criminal Code have been carried forward into the bill.
In paragraphs 7 and 8 of the recommendations in the McRuer report there is reference to the evidence to be given at hearings and the rights of the prisoner and the crown with respect to appeals. These recommendations have been carried into the bill now before the house. The McRuer report also recommended that the courts should be given power to refer a prisoner convicted of any indictable offence for psychiatric examination before sentence. We find that this conclusion has been carried into the bill, and we also find that it applies not only to those classified as dangerous sexual offenders but to prisoners in general.
Conclusion No. 14 in the report of the McRuer commission reads as follows:
The provisions of the law requiring a court to sentence a prisoner found to come within section 661 C.C. to serve a definite term of imprisonment

Criminal Code
before the sentence of preventive detention commences are not consistent with the theory of the law.
Effect has also been given to this conclusion in the bill now before us, with the result that a person may now be sentenced immediately to preventive detention. I do not want to offend against the rules by the discussing the bill clause by clause, and I think it is sufficient for me to make the general comment that the good work done by the McRuer commission has been given effect in the present legislation. There are certain amendments which are not included in the report of the royal commission and there are a number of slight changes in wording, but in general the bill meets a crying need in respect to criminal sexual offenders.
There is another principle introduced in the bill that I should like to discuss. I do not think it was mentioned by previous speakers but it seems to me that it is rather important. It has to do with the power given to a court of summary conviction to remand a prisoner for mental examination. This is found in clause 42 of the bill, and I refer to that clause purely and simply because it deals with one particular principle involved in the bill.
For a good many years magistrates and persons with similar jurisdiction have been remanding for mental examination people about whom they have had some doubts. Heretofore they have had no direct and real authority to do so and no criteria to follow. Under the proposed clause they must secure the opinion of at least one duly qualified medical practitioner, and if the magistrate has reason to believe that a certain accused person may be mentally ill the magistrate now has authority to direct that the person be remanded for observation for a period not exceeding 30 days. I think this clause will be welcomed very much by a great many people involved in the administration of justice because it removes any doubt as to the period and the grounds for which such a remand can be made.
The final principle I should like to discuss has to do with the question of reinstating in the code the provision with respect to dangerous driving. Mention has already been made of this matter by the minister. While the technical reasons for omitting the dangerous driving section from the code when it was rewritten are well known to members of the legal profession, I believe the general public failed to understand the significance. Many people never did quite understand why dangerous driving was no longer an offence. Dangerous driving, of course, always has been an offence, only under a different classification and a different name.

I think the reintroduction of this particular provision in the Criminal Code will do a great deal with respect to the administration of the rules of the road. It has been found that many magistrates, judges and juries hesitate to find a person guilty of criminal negligence in connection with the operation of a motor vehicle. The criminal negligence section was not particularly designed to cover dangerous driving of a motor vehicle; nevertheless it was included as part of the general offence of criminal negligence. Now it is made very clear that dangerous driving of a motor vehicle on the highways is in itself an offence.
Those are the main principles of the bill that I wish to discuss. There are several others, minor in their nature, which can be considered when the bill reaches the committee stage. I think I might say that all these amendments are well considered and should meet with the approval of the house.
