Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to comment on the statement made by the minister which was referred to by the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) when dealing with the question of when and under what circumstances there should be amendments to the Criminal Code.
I am inclined to agree with what the minister has said, provided he underlined the last part of his statement when he intimated that when there was a clear, pressing need and an indicated requirement for amendments, they would be made from time to time without having to wait for a general over-all revision of the provisions of the Criminal Code.
It has been my experience that when you have a body of jurisprudence such as is contained in the various sections of the Criminal Code, administered at varying levels from superior court judges right down to the magisterial level, it is wise not to have it in too great a state of motion and flux. There are many, many hundreds of magistrates who probably deal with by far the greatest percentage of those people charged under the Criminal Code and who have to face a magistrate, judge or judicial tribunal.
When amendments are made in parliament and they percolate down to the magisterial level we usually find some period of time has elapsed before magistrates have acquired an understanding of what is involved in the changes. It may well be that some of the changes become the subject of dispute, as for instance when a case comes before a supreme court judge and is appealed by the crown or the accused. It may even go to the Supreme Court of Canada. Amendments

Criminal Code
which are made today may not be solidified for a period of a year to a year and one half from now.
Consequently I think it is a great mistake to be continually stirring up the provisions of the Criminal Code, because apart from what I have said there are many consequential effects. If we make an amendment to one section of the Criminal Code today we may well find there will be a determination as to the true measure of the results of that amendment by reference to various other sections of the code and by reference to cases which have been decided in the Supreme Court of Canada or the appellate tribunals of the provinces. Sometimes the result is somewhat different from what was anticipated when the amendments left parliament.
Consequently I feel it very wise, when passing amendments in a group such as this, to find out what their impact will be, what consequential amendments may be required later on and what interpretation will be given by our courts. Then after the lapse of two or three years, or whatever the period may be, they should come back for any new amendment which may be required.
I say that I favour that approach provided, and I think the minister made this abundantly clear, we review these amendments if the situation calls for review because of the superior courts' or appellate tribunals' decisions. We should then review these particular amendments, decide that they have a certain meaning and give a certain interpretation to them, because of the great many varying situations which may arise. So long as the department and the minister are prepared to bring in amendments from year to year as and when required, I believe what the minister has announced is proper and wise, and I am saying that from very considerable experience.
I should now like to deal with the question of dangerous sexual offenders. I am not going to go into detail on this matter; it has been commented upon by all speakers so far, and I will have something to say when we are considering this matter in committee. I mention specifically only one aspect of it, and that is with approval. I refer to the effect of the measure which permits there to be some type of treatment without the necessity of there being a determinate jail sentence. I think that is requisite; I think that is very, very necessary. I should only like to make this general observation that this particular aspect of the amendments is a measure of the willingness of this government, and in particular of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) who is charged with the responsibility in these matters, to deal with this question and with kindred problems on a far wider basis than

has been the case in the past, and I am not saying this in any partisan spirit. There is a tremendous wastage in our society today because in the past we have not been prepared to consider ways and means of salvaging persons in this country who have committed criminal offences, and who have done things for which there must be some punishment, but who may still be restored to society. So many of the matters which the government has undertaken, and so many of the bills which have been passed, have indicated that this government is prepared to examine our criminal law in the light of its social implications. While on the one hand preserving penalties which will act as a deterrent, society still holds out a hope of the individual ultimately regaining his place. Those who deliberately choose and persist in criminal courses of action will receive stern punishment but, on the other hand, those who through no fault of their own have fallen into or been driven into a course of action which involves them in the criminal law are to be helped in every way we can. It is not only the pragmatic cost in dollars and cents, if you want to look at it that way, but the fact that these people have a place in society and it is for us to make sure that we restore them to it if possible.
I want to deal to some extent with the amendment which restores to the Criminal Code the section providing for the offence of dangerous driving. I am interested in this matter. I mentioned it on the estimates of the minister and I was very glad to hear at that time that an amendment of this kind was to be included in the amendments to the Criminal Code when they were brought down. At the present time there is in the code the offence of criminal negligence which, when it results in the death of a human being can be punished by life imprisonment. When it results in bodily harm to an individual it can lead to a penalty of up to 10 years, and when committed without any specific harm being done to an individual, an offender is still liable to a penalty of five years. The general description of that offence is "wanton and wilful disregard". It has been my experience, and I am reinforced in it by opinions which have been expressed to me unofficially by members of the judiciary and by crown attorneys who have appeared in these cases that when a judge has to charge a jury giving them direction as to what the law is in respect of criminal negligence and has to explain these words "wanton and wilful disregard" he often runs into difficulty. This situation is made worse when, quite often, a jury, though it is not concerned with the question of the penalty, realizes what the penalty is. Many instances have occurred

when people who should have been convicted in respect to some offence have been acquitted.
Under the old code, under the code as it stood before the introduction of the offence of criminal negligence, there was what is known as reckless driving, as the minister has pointed out, and dangerous driving. Reckless driving can be more or less related to criminal negligence as it now exists. Consequently I think the minister is right in saying it is unnecessary to bring that back into the code. But the reintroduction of this offence and the fact that when there has been a conviction the judge is entitled to prohibit the driver from driving for a specified period of time is an excellent change in the law as it has heretofore existed. The fact that there has been a consequential amendment by which people who are charged with the more serious offence may still be convicted, if the jury sees fit, on the lesser offence of dangerous driving is also to the good. The frightening carnage and slaughter which is taking place on highways of this country- a slaughter which I greatly fear will increase as our population grows and as more cars come upon the highway-will grow no less as more and better roads are built. It is erroneous to think that when we build better roads we shall experience less killings, less motor car accidents, less injuries. I do not think this is the case. Anything we can do to try to stop this and get at the root cause of it is all to the good. That is why I am most heartily in favour of this particular amendment.
I might mention to the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) who brought up what appears to be an excellent suggestion concerning an age limit that this question might well be considered by the provincial authorities. The hon. member was talking about the operation of vessels.
I want to pass on, then, to this particular part of the amendment which introduces into the Criminal Code the various provisions which in the past have been contained in Department of Transport regulations for safety. Apart from the fact that there is involved a question of policing I think it is all to the good that we are now attaching a stigma to these particular actions. In the past it might well be that people regarded them as being a breach of a regulation. Once these regulations become part of the Criminal Code there is likely to be present in the minds of people a consciousness that in committing any of these prohibited acts they are in breach of the criminal law of this country, and it has always been my feeling that when we introduce a provision into the Criminal Code and say it is prohibited and there is a penalty
Criminal Code
for it, reasonable, decent, law abiding people are more likely to consider their actions with care in the future than in the past. For this reason, I feel that the enactment of these particular provisions as part of the Criminal Code will go a long way to ease the situation now existing. And the present situation does present a danger. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) enlarged upon it. Anybody who has been down to the summer resorts, the lakes, the rivers and the seaside of this country in the last few years cannot but be impressed by the large increase in the number of pleasure boats in use. That is part of the heritage of recreation enjoyed by the people of this country. But this is a right which must be used hand in hand with the responsibility which goes with operating vessels of this kind. The waters of this country are for the benefit of all the people. They are not merely for those engaged in operating speed or pleasure boats. I hope the incorporation into the Criminal Code of offences which heretofore were part of the regulations published by the ministry of transport under the small vessels act will go a long way toward dealing with this problem.
The only other point I should like to deal with which has not been mentioned as yet, is that section of the bill dealing with the offence of false pretences. I suggest this proposed legislation enlarges the coverage in respect to banks so as to include other financial institutions and will, I imagine, include credit unions and, in the province of Alberta, the treasury branches which operate there, and will attach to the deliberate writing of cheques on accounts which, known to the writer, do not contain sufficient funds, the same criminal consequences as are now attached to those individuals who write cheques on chartered banks.
I approve of the principles of this legislation as well and feel that when these matters are being dealt with at the committee stage there will be greater opportunity to go into the detail of the principles which have been brought forward.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to be brief because I am not competent to deal with some aspects of this bill. However, I do intend to comment with regard to the two or three sections in which I am particularly interested and with which I feel competent to deal.
I listened to the minister, while enjoying my pipe behind the curtain, with a good deal of interest during his introductory remarks. I noted that he said in his opinion it was not wise to frequently amend the Criminal Code. I think he suggested it should not be amended more frequently than once

Criminal Code
every two years. I feel that is a very sound practice. I feel that the application of law to any degree must be accompanied by time and experience in order to make certain in the first instance that a particular law is not as effective as it should be, and to acquire that experience which indicates the amendments required. I am an individual who is opposed to tinkering with things in too much of a hurry. I am a little old fashioned in that respect. In fact, I have a model T car which is quite serviceable and is much better than many modern vehicles for operation on backwoods roads. I mention that fact to indicate that I do not change my opinions overnight.
I intend to say a few words in regard to clause 5 of this bill dealing with small vessels, which provides for the incorporation in the Criminal Code of the regulations, which previously existed under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport and were enforced by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I think this is a sound move because the field of small vessels navigation is becoming increasingly important. I do not intend to criticize anyone who in past years considered that these regulations were sufficient because the problem in regard to the operation of small vessels has developed very rapidly since the end of the second world war, as a result of a tremendous increase in ownership of small craft for recreational purposes. As I understand the principles of this clause, the administration will be in the hands of provincial authorities, even though the provinces have a contract with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
I have noticed a great increase in the numbers and uses of these small craft on the lakes of the area in which I live. I have been very conscious in recent years of the increase of the horsepower of the engines being used, as well as the increase in interest in water skiing and things of that sort, and I have, therefore, noted the increased necessity for sufficient regulations and laws to deal with the situation.
Without regulations and laws of this kind there will always exist a number of individuals who fail to use good judgment in respect to their own safety, and who have very little regard or concern in some cases for the safety of others, often as a result of ignorance. Many individuals in the last two years have taken to water sports and water recreations with very little experience and knowledge of how very quickly serious accidents can occur through the use of fast moving craft.
As far as the administration of the regulations is concerned one of the big problems will involve personnel. I suggest in isolated

areas, where many people go to enjoy water recreations, it will not be possible to have constables to enforce the regulations. I do not understand how this difficulty will be overcome but I suggest that with the cooperation of launch clubs and recreational organizations it may be possible for provincial authorities to establish services similar to the honorary fire services, members of which, because of their knowledge, and by recommendation of responsible groups, can be issued badges indicating the right to counsel and advise operators of small vessels in the first instance and to turn over to the proper authorities for prosecution the numbers of the craft of individuals who refuse to obey the law. I suggest the success of the application of this law will depend entirely upon co-operation between organizations interested in these types of sports and activities, as well as upon the co-operation of the greater percentage of individuals involved in this type of activity.
In addition to the adoption of these regulations I am of the opinion that small water craft should be licensed. I believe the time has arrived when the owners of small craft should be required to license their vessels at a fee of between $1 and $3, following their having passed rudimentary examinations regarding the principles of navigation and rules of the road, so to speak, as well as an examination in regard to safety requirements, involving the use of life preservers, fire protection equipment, engine control, and things of that sort. I do not know whether this type of regulation would come under the jurisdiction of the federal or provincial government, but I suggest it is something that must be worked out in the very near future through co-operation of the federal Department of Transport and the appropriate provincial authorities.
I make these suggestions, Mr. Speaker, because I am firmly convinced that we have now arrived at the time when operators of small water craft of over three horsepower should be licensed. I think this suggestion will be accepted by the majority of those operators, because it is not the majority who object to regulations and licensing but, like the operators of motor vehicles on the highway, the small percentage of irresponsible individuals who will not be checked or changed except through regulation and licensing.
Mr. Speaker, I should also like to make a few remarks in respect of clause 9 of this bill. Having listened to the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) and the other hon. members of the legal profession who spoke in regard to this bill,

I feel a bit like a duck out of water in doing so. However, clause 9 in part, reads as follows:
(1)	Everyone who. with intent to injure or alarm any person, conveys or causes or procures to he conveyed by letter, telegram, telephone, cable, radio, or otherwise, information that he knows is false is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years.
(2)	Everyone who, with intent to alarm or annoy any person, makes any indecent telephone call to such person is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.
(3)	Everyone who commits an offence under paragraph (b) or (c) of subsection (1) is guilty of (a) an indictable offence and is liable for imprisonment for two years or (b) an offence punishable on summary conviction.
Paragraph (b) and paragraph (c) of subsection (1) read as follows:
(b)	to burn, destroy or damage real or personal property, or
(c)	to kill, main, wound, poison or injure an animal or bird that is the property of any person.
I should like to comment in regard to paragraph (2) of that clause. I can well understand the necessity for the regulations and have known of one or two cases where, in order to annoy, or alarm or cause anxiety to a person, particularly a woman whose husband is away, an individual has telephoned possibly three times per day, week after week, and has simply failed to say anything when the telephone was answered. I have been informed of one case where this has caused serious anxiety and almost a nervous break down. When we come to the clause itself, I wish the minister would inform the house if it covers such a practice where a person simply telephones a number repeatedly night after night and when the phone is answered never speaks. These people do this in order to cause a state of anxiety and annoyance. If it is not covered by the clause, I think it should be because in some instances it is getting to be quite a common trick. It does not sound like much when one mentions it in discussing a clause in a bill but the practice can cause very serious anxiety to some people.
Do you mean to say that sane people do that?

I would not think they were sane, Mr. Speaker, but they are vindictive people or people who want to cause annoyance. We have a small percentage of these cranks, shall I say. It might be done because of certain circumstances, because a person belongs to a certain group or something of that sort, but it does happen.
I come now to clause 11 which I find rather interesting. It is amazing, Mr. Speaker, but even a socialist is attracted to a clause in a bill if it has something to do with his personal experience and if that personal
Criminal Code
experience has cost him some money in the past. We cannot help it. We are all weak and human. The explanatory note in connection with clause 11 reads as follows:
The purpose of this amendment is to make it lawful for a land surveyor, surveying for a public work which will necessarily obliterate an existing boundary mark, to remove such boundary mark provided he establishes a permanent record that permits its original location to be ascertained.
I have known of a number of persons, Mr. Speaker, who suffered considerable inconvenience in recent years because of the removal of a boundary mark or survey stake, particularly with respect to property, timber limits and things of that sort. Mind you, there is an increasing lack of respect for boundary marks. I think some people do not realize what they are, but this situation has been brought about because of the development of highways and public utilities. I have found that the very competent engineers in charge of the building of pipe lines, for example, especially if they come from Texas, have very little regard for these stakes. They simply bring in their bulldozers and push them over.
I think more must be done with regard to this matter. I am not really sure what the offence is but I think it should be considered a serious offence to remove a boundary mark or survey stake. I am not sure what the penalty is either but I wish the minister would inform the house as to the situation when he speaks. I have known of a number of cases in the last four or five years where great inconvenience and considerable expense have been occasioned by people simply pulling up a survey stake at the corner of a timber limit or timber lease and throwing it 10, 15 or even 100 feet into the woods thinking that it is just a joke. This is something that has come about with the increasing population. There are many people who did not grow up under the same environment as we did and they do not realize how much it actually cost to put the stake there.
I am speaking to some extent from personal experience and therefore I speak with some warmth and interest. In the first place, I think this is a very serious offence and attention should be drawn to it even if notices have to be posted for the information particularly of the younger people who are quite unaware of what they are doing. They think these stakes are simply driven in at appropriate intervals and can easily be put back in place. They do not realize that it may require the running of four or five miles of line to locate the stake again.
It is explained here that the purpose of this amendment is to make it lawful for a land surveyor, surveying for a public work which will necessarily obliterate an existing boundary mark, to remove such boundary mark

Criminal Code
provided he establishes a permanent record that permits its original location to be ascertained. I have seen that sort of thing done in the past and I am not sure whether it is sufficient. I think it should be a last resort. I think that anyone who removes a stake or boundary mark should first be required, if at all possible, to provide an offset mark. What I mean by that is that if you put blazes on three trees and triangulate from the three trees you can find the location of the stake even if it has burned down. In the majority of cases you can locate the boundary mark or offset stake or offset monument, whether the distance is 10 feet or 50 feet or 100 feet. That is a much less expensive way of determining the corner or boundary of any property than depending on a record which will cause you to hire a surveyor at considerable expense who, in order to locate that position, may have to run a line two or three miles long. I am speaking of large land holdings, timber holdings and things of that sort.
I ask the minister to consider whether it is not possible first of all to provide for an offset boundary mark in order to lessen the expense rather than having to determine the location of the boundary mark or stake from a record. I have no doubt that the minister has received advice on this matter but I just mention these things as a result of my experience. When we come to this clause I should like him to tell me whether there is any merit in the suggestion or what reasons he has for refusing it.
When it comes to the question of what is a permanent mark, that is a very relative term. In surveying history a four-inch by four-foot stake was a permanent mark according to the legislature of British Columbia. Under modern conditions a wooden stake is no longer a permanent mark and I think there should be some elaboration of the word "permanent" to indicate that it means either an iron stake or a cement block or something else that is definitely permanent and cannot be easily wrenched out or destroyed by fire or because of other circumstances.
These are the clauses in which I am partic-ularily interested, Mr. Speaker, though I am interested in all these amendments. I am very pleased to see the amendment with respect to dangerous driving. I listened with great interest to the minister's explanation of the amendments concerning sexual offenders. I am going to say very little on that subject because I am not competent to deal with the legal, medical and psychological aspects of such a very complicated problem. I judge from the minister's remarks that this is a progressive step and an improvement

over the former legislation. I know the matter has received considerable study and is of great importance.
Finally, with respect to this serious problem which requires our sympathetic attention, I wish to say that I am all in favour of this new and more sympathetic approach. While we have to protect citizens and restrict and punish those who are criminals in this respect, we also realize there are many persons who are actually psychologically sick and who suffer as a result of their inherited tendencies or unfortunate environment. This group is very pleased to see these amendments and we will watch the results with interest. Those members in particular who have taken an interest in this subject for many years will watch with interest the application of this new law respecting sexual offenders. No doubt as a result of time and experience amendments will be found necessary to improve the legislation further, but from our point of view this is a step in the right direction.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. B. Nesbitt (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) for the amendments to the Criminal Code which he has introduced. In my opinion all of them have been needed for some time but, as the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) has said, it is not wise to tinker with these things until proper consideration has been given. While I should like to speak on a number of the amendments, I think I will confine my remarks at this time to those involving the regulation of small vessels. This, Mr. Speaker, has been a matter of great interest to me ever since I have been in this house. The history of this legislation is probably interesting, too. In 1954 I had the honour of introducing a resolution concerning the establishment of a search and rescue organization on the inland waters of Canada. This resolution was debated on several occasions and received the support of all hon. members who spoke. Naturally, the discussion of this resolution covered a rather wide area and included, among other things, the regulation of small vessels on inland waters.
Subsequently, amendments were made to the Canada Shipping Act to regulate small vessels. I can well recall that many hon. members in this house now, as well as others who were members at that time, contributed many valuable suggestions to the committee which was set up in 1955 and 1956. As one or two hon. members have pointed out today, while regulations were passed under the appropriate section of the Canada Shipping Act, there has been some confusion in various

parts of the country as to how these regulations should be enforced. In Ontario, for example, the provincial police were not certain as to whether they should enforce them or whether the Royal Canadian Mounted Police should enforce them, since the regulations were made under a federal statute. Certainly in so far as the public is concerned, the regulations under the Canada Shipping Act relating to small vessels have not been very adequately enforced. I think all hon. members would agree with this.
While the enforcement of the law is of course not the responsibility of this parliament, nevertheless now that these regulations are embodied in the Criminal Code it will be made quite clear that the provincial authorities should enforce these regulations the same as other sections of the code. The hon. member for Kootenay West made a suggestion with regard to enforcement. He said that yacht clubs and organizations of that nature might very well appoint special deputies to help enforce these regulations during the summer months. I would agree with this suggestion. However, I should like to go a step further. Since the use of small craft is, of course, prevalent in the summer months, those who are charged with responsibility for enforcing these regulations might very well give consideration to the employment of senior university students. This scheme would provide the students with summer employment, with the necessary funds to continue their education, and at the same time would not cause the law enforcement authorities to take on an unnecessary number of persons whose services would not be required during the balance of the year. As I have already mentioned, services of this nature would be required largely during the summer months. I know that the Department of National Revenue employs senior university students to assist in the enforcement of customs regulations during the summer. I feel that the provincial authorities who will be responsible for enforcing these regulations might very well deputize a number of senior university students to help enforce the regulations covering small craft on the great lakes, Muskoka lakes and other resort areas in Ontario as well as other parts of Canada.
There is another matter to which reference has been made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) as well as the hon. member for Kootenay West, and that is the question of licensing small craft and the age limits of operators. I realize that there may be some difficulty in setting age restrictions. Also, I do not know whether or not this parliament has the constitutional authority to license boats. This is a subject for constitutional lawyers, and I 90205-6-414
Criminal Code
would not presume to make a statement upon it. I would be interested in hearing what the Minister of Justice might have to say on the matter. If it is not possible for this parliament to legislate on the matter, perhaps the appropriate legislative bodies could do so.
I refer, of course, to the question of licensing not only small craft, which I believe are licensed now, but licensing the people who operate them. I am not particularly concerned whether a one dollar or two dollar fee is charged, as suggested; I do not believe that is important. The important thing is to make certain that the people who operate small craft which have engines of high horsepower are persons who are responsible. In so far as the age limit is concerned, I do not know what it should be. I feel this should be given careful consideration. Perhaps sixteen would be the appropriate age, just as it is for driving a car. One thing is quite certain. Since the war there has been a great increase in the number of small pleasure craft using our inland waters. I believe it is just as essential to regulate craft using these waters as it is to regulate traffic on the highways. I believe that is a selfevident fact upon which I do not have to elaborate.
Some consideration should be given, too, to requiring persons to be a certain age before they are permitted to operate boats which are propelled by engines of perhaps more than three horsepower. These boats can become very dangerous weapons indeed in the hands of irresponsible persons. Provision is made, I see, for adults, for those who are intoxicated while operating boats. I have spent a great deal of time on the inland waters during the summer because boating happens to be a hobby of mine. Generally, the worst offenders in the operation of small boats are young boys and girls of 10, 12 or 13 years of age. It is true there is the occasional adult offender. However, all too frequently we see children of eight or ten years of age operating boats powered by engines of 40 horsepower. They go roaring around small lakes, in around swimmers, in a very dangerous manner. I do not believe there is any excuse for the parents who permit this to happen. I believe an age limit might be set which would prohibit children operating a boat over a certain horsepower.
It is very difficult, of course, to make children reponsible and punish them because they are not really responsible. I believe provision might be made for the punishment in some way of the parents who permit children to operate small boats of high horsepower. This matter should be given consideration. I do not expect the minister to immediately produce an additional amendment to the act because, as the hon. member for Kootenay

Criminal Code
West pointed out, you do not want to tinker with the Criminal Code unless adequate consideration has been given to the amendments. I think this is something the officials of the minister and of the Department of Transport might carefully consider because I believe such provisions would go a long way toward preventing unpleasant accidents. I believe those are all the observations I have to make at this time.

should like to ask a question, Mr. Speaker. What is the meaning of the words "dangerous to navigation" contained in section 226A (1)? What kind of navigation is included? I understand the reference to be wholly to power boats, those little boats that rush about as the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) has said at 30 to 40 miles an hour and make life hideous for everybody within range. Is any consideration being given to the comfort and security of those strange people who still row or paddle or sail or are they regarded as being just as extinct as the dodo? Are they no longer to have any rights? Are we quite prepared to accept the fact that those sports have now given way to the so-called sport of sitting in a boat and being rushed about by an engine? That is my question. In the consideration of the words "dangerous to navigation", can the navigation of these innocent people be considered, because it certainly is no joke to suggest that it is dangerous for them to be on their lawful occasions when these incredibly powerful little boats with irresponsible people in them are dashing about.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to deal with the principle of this bill and to congratulate most heartily my colleague from Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) who replied to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) this morning, even though she hardly had any time to prepare herself.
I should like to offer similar congratulations to my colleague from Maisonneuve-Rose-mont (Mr. Deschatelets) who, in spite of the few hours at his disposal, succeeded in giving us this afternoon a most accurate statement on the bill under consideration.
Since I have been sitting in this house, Mr. Speaker, I have taken part in several debates on bills introduced by the Minister of Justice. I had the opportunity also of participating in the debate which takes place each time we consider the estimates of the Department of Justice, the penitentiaries division and the R.C.M.P.
Very seldom did I have to address any reproach to the Minister of Justice but this time, I have a few to make. Perhaps those reproaches do not concern him in particular but they surely concern the government of which he is a member, and especially the leader of the house.
During his speech this morning the Minister of Justice told us that, in his opinion, a government should not introduce amendments to the Criminal Code every year but rather think them out thoroughly and submit them to the house deliberately, after having considered all the aspects of one or several matters covered by the Criminal Code.
Mr. Speaker, I agree in part with the principle that legislation, and especially the Criminal Code, should not be amended without due consideration. On the other hand, the government, clearly disregarding this principle, introduces through the agency of the Minister of Justice a bill including 46 sections. This bill was read for the first time Saturday morning, and it is only this morning, at the beginning of the sitting, that a copy of the bill was made available to us. And moreover, Mr. Speaker, the standing orders of this house provide that any bill must be printed both in French and in English.
Now, when this morning's order paper was distributed, the French version of the bill was not ready. In fact, when we came to the house at 11 o'clock this morning, only the English version was available, and we had to send over for the French version.
It is extremely important for hon. members, particularly the French speaking members, to prepare themselves adequately for a debate. It would have been preferable to be able to examine the French text at the outset. We did not even have a single week end to consider this bill, and you will agree that this is inadequate.
This is what I would call an omnibus bill, as the amendments put forward deal with various aspects of the Criminal Code.
I have no doubt that these amendments have been the subject of continuing and thorough studies by the minister and his officials. Some time was also devoted to them by various organizations. I refer in particular to the Canadian association of police chiefs, which made recommendations in a brief submitted to the minister last March.
The proposed amendments to the Criminal Code deal with the dangerous driving of motor vehicles, threats made by telephone or otherwise, etc.
fMr. Nesbitt.]

The McRuer commission, appointed in 1954 by the former government, pursued its studies until 1958, when it submitted its report.
It recommended various amendments to the Criminal Code, particularly in relation to habitual criminals and habitual sexual offenders.
We agree with the minister that all amendments proposed in his bill represent a step in the right direction. As far as I am concerned, I foresee no difficulty in getting this bill adopted.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, before resuming my seat, to deal with a few points covering dangerous sexual offenders.
They are divided into two categories.
First of all there are the sexual perverts, the depraved individuals, who are caught in the swamp of sexual delinquency. We all admit with the minister that they have to be kept away from society.
On the other hand, there are sick people, those who suffer from an anomalous state for which they are not actually responsible.
Those people are not necessarily criminals. But, in their case, the state has the responsibility to provide a temporary internment which would help their rehabilitation.
Some time ago rehabilitation was discussed in this house, particularly when the estimates of the penitentiaries branch were discussed.
Last Monday, more particularly, when we examined the penitentiaries bill, the question was studied at length. Habitual criminals, ordinary habitual criminals, which this legislation covers, and dangerous sexual offenders were all discussed.
Clause 39 of this bill says that the minister shall, at least once a year, submit all cases of criminals undergoing preventive detention to a review by the parole board.
To my mind this is an improvement. The Criminal Code now provides for a revision every three years, but this bill provides a yearly revision of the records of those unfortunate people.
With regard to the rehabilitation angle, the minister mentioned it when the situation of penitentiaries was discussed.
I believe that, in a general way, this section, if it is enacted as we may expect, will mean a substantial improvement and a better protection of society against those who live in ordinary crime or sexual crime.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal briefly with section
90205-fi-414 J
Criminal Code
660 dealing with applications for the imposition of preventive detention. Section 660 reads as follows:
Where an accused has been convicted-
Section 661 contains the same words. Section 661 deals with cases of rape, carnal knowledge, indecent assault on female, buggery or bestiality, indecent assault on male and gross indecency. These are cases which are usually heard by juries. One of the sections provides that the application for the imposition of preventive detention shall not be heard by a jury. Then section 662 provides:
(a) an application under subsection (1) of section 660 shall not be heard unless. ..
(ii) seven clear days' notice has been given to the accused by the prosecutor, either before or after conviction or sentence-
Therefore I am a bit puzzled whether the application can be heard concurrently with the offence being tried, because in most instances the offence would be tried by a jury. It is provided that notice may be served even before conviction, although sections 660 and 661 provide that application may be made only after an accused has been convicted. I submit that this bill requires amendment to reconcile those two sections.
Another section provides that if the application is made after conviction it shall not be heard by the convicting judge. That would imply that a transcription of the evidence would be required for the hearing of the application. Past experience has shown that many times an accused has not been able to properly defend himself because he did not have the funds or opportunity to obtain for himself a transcription of the evidence.
Then section 667 deals with the right of appeal to the court of appeal. Here again 1 should like to underline the fact that an accused has to face an almost indefinite sentence of imprisonment, if he is convicted and sentenced to preventive detention, and he may not have the funds with which to provide the transcription of evidence.
We know that cases are dismissed every year in the court of appeal where the accused has filed notice of appeal but has not the means to provide a transcription of the evidence for all the judges of the court of appeal, for the crown and himself. I believe accused persons deserve some protection in this regard, because it means that wealth and poverty are not balanced. Many times an accused has not sufficient funds of his own with which to provide the required number of transcriptions, and very often he has not any friends who can provide these funds. I commend the minister for this bill, but it seems to me more safeguards should be provided for accused persons.

Criminal Code

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on Bill No. C-110 at the present time I do not wish to delay the bill being considered in committee. Although there is no general principle involved in this mil, it contains a number of substantial amendments to various sections of the Criminal Code.
I listened with a great deal of interest this morning to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) as he outlined the provisions of this bill, particularly those sections dealing with dangerous sexual offenders. I believe that in this particular field the provisions of our Criminal Code at the present time are wholly inadequate. It is not enough to remove these people from society; we must, if we are going to practice the principles of Christianity, try to provide some means of rehabilitating them.
I also agree with the minister that amendments to the Criminal Code should not be made piecemeal, they should not be made haphazardly or too often unless it is absolutely necessary. It has been found in the past that one amendment to the Criminal Code usually requires several other amendments to various other sections. If those amendments are not made at the time the result is that the new amendments, if enforced by the courts without the corresponding sections being amended-perhaps this is a good thing for defence counsel-possibly a person who should have been convicted escapes punishment.
There are a number of substantial amendments in this bill. As the bill will be discussed section by section in committee I do not intend to refer to these sections specifically, except to say I am quite disturbed about introducing into the Criminal Code regulations dealing with the operation of small vessels.
As I read the relevant section, it puts small vessels in exactly the same position as motor vehicles on our highways. In the constituency of Charlotte we are not particularly concerned with pleasure craft except in some of the inland waters. As this house is aware, we have tides of 28 feet and 29 feet in the bay of Fundy which prevent the use of that water by pleasure craft.
Also, most of the vessels in the bay of Fundy area are commercial vessels used entirely for fishing purposes, having a speed of possibly six or seven knots per hour, and some of them a great deal less. Most of these boats are powered by inboard motors, except the small boats used by fishermen for lobster fishing, which are sometimes powered by small outboard motors. These boats do not constitute any menace, or any of the dangers that this provision of the code contemplates
[Mr. Regnier.l
and I would suggest to the minister that possibly there should be some distinction made between commercial craft and pleasure craft.
I have another observation to make. During the past number of years, particularly since the present code was revised in 1955, there has been a tendency to take away from an accused person the right to a trial by jury. I realize there was a reason for this. It has prevented a lot of minor cases from going up before the supreme court or before a county court and a jury. Nevertheless, we should keep in mind that when we are going to impose a severe penalty on a person charged with a criminal offence we must give him an ample opportunity so that he may have a proper defence at the right time. We have, in other words, extended the powers of magistrates without, in a good many instances, increasing their competence. I realize that the appointment of magistrates is purely a matter for provincial governments, but we have an instance in this bill where we are going to make driving by a motor or a boat operator whose licence is under suspension an indictable offence carrying with it a possible penalty of two years' imprisonment, yet we are making it one of the offences which can be tried by a magistrate with absolute jurisdiction. In other words, although the magistrate now, under the summary conviction penalty section, can sentence a man on conviction to a maximum of $500 and six months, or a fine or sentence less than the maximum it is now going to be made an indictable offence when a man is liable for two years imprisonment, yet an accused has no option but to be tried by the magistrate. Under the absolute jurisdiction section of the code we find that the offences dealt with in this way are more or less minor offences such as assault, assault on officers or peace officers, attempted theft, thefts involving sums less than $50 and so on, most of which are dealt with by magistrates by the imposition of fines or short jail sentences of maybe up to 30 days. If the circumstances surrounding the suspension of a licence in the operation of a car or a boat after suspension were serious enough, I suggest an offender could be tried under the criminal negligence section of the code.
I was interested in the minister's observations on the old dangerous driving section of the Criminal Code which, if my memory serves me correctly, was section 285(6). The minister explained why this section was deleted, but I would suggest that the main reason was the difficulty of obtaining convictions under the old code which set out three distinct and separate offences. I am pleased to see that the change now proposed

in this bill deletes many of the objectionable features of the old section 285(6). But I think this further question should be raised: are we not getting into another field of conflict, as most of the provinces have passed legislation dealing with the operation of motor vehicles? These are usually called "due care" sections. I just point this out to the minister to indicate that there is some difficulty inherent in this section.
I do not intend to discuss at any great length habitual criminals or dangerous sexual offenders. I suggest, however, that in both categories the federal government should provide some means of rehabilitating individuals of this type, providng ways and means whereby they can obtain the necessary training. It has been my experience over the years to defend a good many of these people and I say they are more to be pitied than punished. I feel we are failing in our duty if we do not provide not only for their removal from society but some method whereby worthy citizens can be made of them.
I shall have some further observations to make when the bill is before the committee and is being discussed clause by clause. I feel I should commend the minister and his department for the substantial and beneficial amendments proposed in this bill.

Mr. Speaker, in any properly organized society, criminal law must be conceived so as to protect the citizens, and any legislation must always be drafted in the light of common good.
If we consider the bill now before us, we are convinced once again that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) has taken into account various recommendations submitted to him by different organizations.
This bill, on the whole, features three aspects of safety. First, there is the section dealing with highway safety; the second section provides for water or maritime safety; and third, a series of sections provide for moral or social safety.
Considering the dangers incidental to driving nowadays on our increasingly congested highways, I feel we must take stricter steps to bring to reason those who drive their vehicle without paying any heed to the rights of those they meet on the highways. In view of the large number of accidents, the legislators must punish those who break our laws because, by their reckless and dangerous driving, they ruin the social order in families.
Criminal Code
Besides, I believe we are right in being even stricter with those who, because of carelessness, youth, stupidity or intoxication constitute real hazards to public safety.
The minister has decided to include in this legislation the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act with which the people were not familiar enough and which were not respected unfortunately. There again, there are too many water casulties today and society which we represent, must take every possible means to put an end to this lack of care which people show much too often on our lakes and rivers during the summer season. Turning offences under the Shipping Act into indictable offences appears to me to be a wise measure in so far as it will prompt owners of commercial and pleasure crafts to observe basic safety rules.
I think we must pass such a measure in order to provide the ever increasing number of people who are to be found on our beaches, rivers and lakes with a minimum of safety and to protect them from the fools who, careless of what is going on around them, are a real threat to the public.
The principal feature of Bill No. C-110 is the provision dealing with dangerous sexual offenders. It seems that the bill wants these offenders against marality to be treated more like sick persons.
The legislation aims at protecting youth against these mentally unbalanced and dangerous beings; that is why the minister inserted into the bill these provisions the effects of which will be to protect society from these dangerous persons.
The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Regnier) seemed to view the problem from a different angle. In his opinion, offences mentioned in sections 136, 138, 141, 147 and 148 of the Criminal Code are still crimes for a jury to judge. And when the hon. member said that the application cannot be heard by a jury, he was referring to a distinction bearing not on the crime itself, but on the consequences that the individual might bring upon himself in committing his crime, because the attorney general must decide on the application of this act and he may order an inquiry before a judge to determine whether the accused is a dangerous sexual offender. It is only in that case that the hearing is not before a jury. In my opinion, the person who has to face a specific charge against morality retains all his means of defence, as it is the case now under our Criminal Code as modified in 1955.

Criminal Code
All members will readily accept those different amendments which not only help improve our Criminal Code but ensure a larger measure of protection for society through fuller respect for the individual and the right to human life.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the remarks of hon. members who have spoken this afternoon in regard to Bill No. C-110 as introduced this morning by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton). I listened with particular interest to the remarks of the minister, and the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), my neighbour on the other side of the house, whose words are usually wise and worthy of attention. I thought this was particularly true when he referred to the matter of amendments to the Criminal Code, that very important piece of legislation in this country which applies throughout the many provinces, and involves all the people of Canada.
The hon. member for Peace River pointed out that certain amendments must be made to the Criminal Code from time to time because of the fact that our way of life changes, as well as because of changes in our society. He suggested that the amendments to our legislation must reflect these changes but that they should not be made too quickly or too often, because they must be interpreted throughout this land by the members of the judiciary who are, after all, human also, as well as by lawyers engaged both in crown and defence work. Time must be given, as that hon. member pointed out, for interpretation of the changes, and for cases to be tried in the various courts of the land, so that a complete picture can be obtained as to the impact upon our society. We must not be stagnant in regard to our legislation, but must at the same time allow for a period of interpretation.
I should like to make a few remarks regarding the amendment contained in this bill particularly concerning the operation of small boats. I feel it has particular importance to the Atlantic provinces, and recognize the situation referred to by the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stewart), and the importance of this legislation to the people of his area where there exists a particular problem because of the fact that small boats are engaged to a great extent in commercial enterprises. However, I suggest that small boats are used a great deal today in many other areas in the Atlantic provinces, as well as in the areas of inland water in Canada.

I feel that the results of these regulations, formerly contained under the shipping act, will justify their incorporation in the Criminal Code.
I think that the benefits of this change will be recognized by the many individuals throughout Canada who operate small boats strictly for enjoyment and in the pursuit of hobbies, as well as by those individuals who are members of yacht clubs and other similar organizations. I am sure those individuals will also realize the necessity of having regulations of this type. I do not suggest that they should be too strict, but I believe that responsible individuals will recognize the necessity for regulations in respect of this type of operation as responsible car drivers throughout this country recognize the need of highway and traffic regulations.
In regard to the amendment reinstating the dangerous driving section of the code, I suggest this is one of the amendments I had in mind at the opening of my remarks this afternoon when I referred to the necessity of keeping our legislation in line with changes in our way of life and society, for the protection of our citizens. This bill also provides that a charge of criminal negligence can be reduced to a charge of dangerous driving. I suggest to the minister that he give consideration to the remarks made by the hon. member for Charlotte regarding subsection (3) of section 225, covering the operation of a vehicle by a disqualified individual. I shall not refer to this in detail now, but may do so at the committee stage. It seems rather strange to me that under this provision an individual is liable to two years' imprisonment upon conviction of an indictable offence because, as the hon. member for Charlotte pointed out, the matter of dangerous driving is one which is within the absolute jurisdiction of a magistrate, so that an accused person cannot elect to be tried by a judge or a judge and jury. Perhaps the minister will consider this situation and give some explanation in his reply.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) mentioned the fact that he owns a model T car. I should hope that he drives it at an adequate speed because, should he not drive it fast enough, although he would not be in contravention of the dangerous driving section, he would undoubtedly be dealt with under the provincial motor vehicle act of the province of British Columbia.
That hon. member also mentioned the legislation referring to the making of telephone calls to the annoyance or nuisance of individuals. It has come to my attention that quite often calls are made and when the phone is answered the person on the other

end of the line hangs up, thus creating a great nuisance. I realize it is very difficult to check through the telephone companies and prove such matters but I would suggest to the minister that perhaps he might look into the nuisance that is caused with a view to doing something about it in the future.
The legislation with regard to sexual offences has been discussed fully and I do not intend to go into it. There are also amendments with regard to election involving offences where absolute jurisdiction has rested with the magistrate, and there are other matters of importance dealt with in the bill.
I do not wish to take any more time now except to say that the amendments with regard to sexual offences and the other changes in the Criminal Code that have been made since the minister became Minister of Justice show that he is carrying out a policy of attempting to rehabilitate many of the offenders and is making an effort to restore them to society as worth-while citizens. When the bill is discussed in committee there may be other matters of interest which I will have an opportunity to discuss further then.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a number of important points which have been of some value have been made in the discussion and I wish to express my appreciation to all hon. members who have spoken for their suggestions which I am sure will be helpful to us when considering whether or not there are some amendments that should be made in committee. I also wish to express appreciation to all hon. members for their general indication of the support which the proposals embodied in the bill are receiving and will receive in all parts of the house. I will endeavour, as I think I should in recognition of the serious contributions that have been made, to deal with the majority, if not all, of the points that have been made, but if I omit any or omit reference to any hon. member particularly I would ask all hon. members to understand that this may well be because the same points in different form were made by a number of members and also because some of them lend themselves perhaps better to detailed consideration in committee. However, I wish to show hon. members, who have been very generous to me, the courtesy of dealing with all the points that have been made.
The hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) referred first to the important aspect of the new provision with regard to
Criminal Code
the small boat laws which concerns the question of enforcement by the provinces. I should like to assure her that there have been some discussions with the provinces, most particularly with the province of Ontario. It will be appreciated, of course, that in all provinces except Ontario and Quebec the provincial police service is provided by the R.C.M.P., and to some extent therefore the question of whether they are enforced under provincial or federal regulations is but a variation of the same problem in those provinces.
As was pointed out, it will be largely a question of whether or not adequate personnel can be provided for the discharge of this very heavy duty, a duty made particularly difficult because of the fact that the use of these boats mushrooms during the summer months and then falls off to practically nothing, at least on the inland waters of Canada, during the winter months. The problem, therefore, is one of having sufficient personnel to deal with the matter in the summer tourist months while not having so many men on your force that you have got nothing for them to do in the other months of the year.
In that connection I was particularly impressed with a suggestion made by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) that it might well be that some type of honorary or voluntary warden could be appointed and given some authority at any rate in connection with the enforcement of these laws. I am much struck with that suggestion and I have made a note to investigate, the moment I have time, the question of whether such persons, for instance, as game wardens might not be persons to whom it would be appropriate to give authority in this field. I would think that in a large number of cases, if not the majority, boats being used at resorts would be used in areas where there is a game warden or fisheries warden present. Therefore this strikes me as being a very excellent and apt suggestion.
In addition to the discussions which the R.C.M.P. have had with the provinces, I should point out that the Department of Transport has also had some preliminary discussions with the provinces regarding this whole matter and that it is their intention to follow up these discussions and have specific talks on the problem of licensing. I noted that all members, I believe, who referred to the small boat problem, referred to the question of licensing the operators of boats. It will be appreciated, of course, that here you have a question where we have to be careful because of the limits of constitutional authority, and it might well be that the licensing of boats is something which is

Criminal Code
within the authority of the provinces. In any event, it is desired and intended to discuss this question, and when and if a licensing system is worked out there can then be provision either that to operate a boat without a licence is a criminal offence, which could be provided subsequently, or if the licensing were to be done under provincial authority the provinces themselves could provide, in a manner similar to that which now prevails in the highway acts of the provinces, that the operation of a boat without a licence is an offence. We have very much in mind the desirability of working out a licensing system and then providing by the appropriate provincial or federal legislation that to operate a boat without a licence is an offence. Here again, of course, there would be room to take care of that point which many members raised that it is probably desirable to impose an age limit as a qualification for the operation of a boat with an engine say of more than three horsepower.
The hon. member for Niagara Falls referred also to the question of habitual criminals and the changes imported into the law by the bill now before the house. So that she will not think that I am omitting anything in the discussion, I should point out that one of the problems she referred to does not arise, I think, by reason of the fact that an application to have a person declared an habitual criminal or a dangerous sexual offender is not now heard by a jury. It is heard by a judge alone and the only change we are making in this respect is to provide that where the application is made subsequent to a conviction it should not be heard by the judge or magistrate who tried the specific offence which gave rise to the application.
I was also asked for the record with respect to habitual criminals and sexual offenders. The following are the records as of June 19, 1961, with respect to persons sentenced as habitual criminals. The total number sentenced was 54. The number who died in prison was four, leaving a total of 50. Of that number, 24 had been released on parole. Of the 24 released, four had had their parole revoked or forfeited, so that there are in custody or were in custody 30 habitual criminals. Of those 30, one had successfully appealed his conviction. As of this date, the actual number in custody was 29. The record with regard to parole is, as I have pointed out, 24 have been released on parole. Two have subsequently died; four have had their parole revoked or forfeited, so that there are actually 18 habitual criminals on parole at the present time.
The record of criminal sexual psychopaths, again as of June 19 this year, is as follows; The total number of persons sentenced under

that provision was 34. Of those, one had died in prison and nine had been released on parole. Of those nine, one had had his parole revoked or forfeited. There is, in custody at the present time under this provision, a total of 25 persons. Of those, one is appealing his conviction. Again, with respect to the record of the parolees, of the eight released on parole, one has subsequently died; one has had his parole revoked; one is in custody facing other charges. There are, therefore, five at present on parole who had previously been sentenced as criminal sexual psychopaths.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rose-mont (Mr. Deschatelets) referred to the small boat regulations, and particularly the problem of young persons operating small boats. I hope he will agree that I have covered that and when a licensing system is worked out, which I think is most desirable, it will be possible to cover the question of those who should be licensed to operate boats with engines beyond a certain horsepower.
The hon. member for Kootenay West dealt also with this problem. I have noted his suggestion regarding temporary personnel being appointed with authority under these regulations. He asked me some questions concerning the penalty for removing boundary markers. This is found in section 384 of the code, and the maximum penalty at the present time, if I recall correctly, is five years. The section reads:
Everyone who wilfully pulls down, defaces, alters or removes
(a) a boundary mark . . .
is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for five years.
The maximum penalty for this offence is quite severe at the present time. However, it is a fact that with the number of roads being built, and the widths and permanence of these roads, an increasing problem has been posed for surveys in that at the present time the code merely protects them where they carefully replace the necessary boundary mark as it was. With the type and size of highway being built now, it is becoming increasingly difficult to replace the mark where the surveyor took it up. It is for this reason the additional provision protecting the surveyor is being enacted, so that if he finds it impossible to replace the boundary mark he will be covered if he establishes a permanent record of the original position sufficient to permit such position to be ascertained.
I would think that with respect to the hon. member's point the surveyors should be required merely to establish reference marks so that it would not be necessary to run a line two or three miles in length to establish

the location of the original mark, the surveyors would be aware of this and would be inclined to establish such reference marks. There is nothing in the wording of the clause that would preclude that. I believe the wording of the clause suggests this. It says he is protected where he establishes a permanent record of the original position sufficient to permit such position to be ascertained. An offsetting mark would be the most readily means of establishing the original position. I will give consideration to the matter. I am unable to give my hon. friend a firm answer at this time, but I shall be glad to give consideration to it to see whether in committee or at perhaps some other appropriate time, a clarification is indicated.
The hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) also commented on the necessity and desirability of licensing operators of boats. We have, I think, covered that point sufficiently now.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Mac-donnell) raised the interesting and understandable point of the protection of those who are operators of small boats but who operate them without engines preferring-I am glad there are numbers in this country who do so prefer-to operate them with their own muscle power or by sail. He asked whether they would be protected by the words "dangerous to navigation". I would say they would be because he will note the section provides:
Everyone who navigates or operates a vessel or any water skis... in a manner that is dangerous to navigation, life or limb... is guilty of an indictable offence-*
If the operator or owner of a boat with a powerful engine goes sweeping past at a speed which endangers the life or limb of my hon. friend or others who share his commendable point of view, and there is danger of swamping the rowboat or sailboat, then there would be an offence under this section as we have drafted it.
The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Regnier) raised a question as to whether it would not be desirable to provide more protection for the accused in connection with an application to have a man declared either a dangerous sexual offender or an habitual criminal. He suggested that it might be provided that the jury which heard the case should also dispose of the application. We had thought rather that the opposite principle should govern on the grounds that where a jury had also heard and disposed of a case- the application would not arise unless the accused had been convicted of that specific charge-it would then be undesirable to have the same court which had convicted on the specific charge deal with the application to
Criminal Code
have him declared a dangerous offender or habitual criminal. I want to remind the house again that these applications will not be dealt with by a jury in any event. The principle which we think should be applicable is that the judge who disposed of the charge on which the accused was convicted should not dispose of the application under this section because of the possibility of prejudice to the accused. We thought it should be a new judge or magistrate as the case may be.
The hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stewart) suggested that there should be some words in clause 5 of the bill to make it clear that the provision does not apply to commercial vessels but only to small, pleasure craft. I would be glad to give this matter further consideration but I must say that at first sight the suggestion does not appeal to me. After all, the offence that we are now importing into the criminal law is the navigation of a vessel in a manner that is dangerous to life or limb. I am not able to appreciate why commercial vessels should be exempt or placed in another class so that this provision would not apply to them.
I point out further for the hon. member's consideration that it is provided by a later subsection that, with respect to commercial vessels which are required to carry certificated masters, mates or engineers, the right of those persons to operate a commercial vessel cannot be taken away by a conviction under this section. The reason for that is that it is the Canada Shipping Act that at present provides for the qualifications of persons who shall have certificates as masters, mates or engineers. We think that is the proper place where those provisions should rest and that the taking away from one of these persons of his right to operate a vessel for which he is certificated should remain under the shipping act. What is intended here is that if a person operates a vessel, whether it be a commercial craft or a pleasure craft, in a manner that is dangerous to navigation or life or limb, then he commits a criminal offence; and if he is the owner and operator of a pleasure craft he may be prohibited from operating that craft. However, if he is the certificated master, mate or engineer of a commercial vessel, then the question of whether or not he has his certificate taken away from him rests to be disposed of under the Canada Shipping Act.
Then the hon. member for Charlotte and also the hon. member for Pictou both raised the question as to whether it is wise to provide, as we have provided in subclause 2 of clause 4, that a charge of operating a motor vehicle while disqualified or prohibited from driving by reason of a previous conviction,

Criminal Code
should be made an indictable offence as well as an offence punishable on summary conviction as it is now. The reason for their concern, if I understood them correctly, is that this was an offence within the absolute jurisdiction of a magistrate and that to provide that it is now also an indictable offence would have the effect of giving to magistrates, about whose qualifications there are sometimes some reservations, the power to impose punishments of two years and more. With respect I think I must take issue with the hon. gentlemen. I have not had time to check this matter out completely since it was raised, but it is my impression that this charge would not be within the absolute jurisdiction of a magistrate. It may be that the offence for which they were originally convicted and on the basis of that conviction were prohibited from driving was within the absolute jurisdiction of the magistrate. However, I question whether the charge which is involved here, namely the charge of driving a motor vehicle while under an order of prohibition, is under the absolute jurisdiction of a magistrate. The study I gave to it in the few moments since the question was raised rather persuades me that it is only triable by a magistrate with consent. If that is correct-and I will have a further check made on that matter-it would, I hope, dispose of the reservations expressed by my hon. friends.
I think that covers the points that were raised, Mr. Speaker. If I have left any out or if I have not covered them adequately I shall try to make amends when we are in committee on the clauses.
