speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?
Question.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Flynn in the chair.
On clause 1.

By virtue of the fact that the bill has not been given to us in time for us to make a very detailed study of it and also by virtue of the fact that, as I have no doubt, the minister has brought in the amendments as a result of some difficulties which have been created in the past and recommendations which have been made, may I ask that the minister, as we approach each group of sections dealing with different subjects, give us some background on what the present law is, why it has not been found to be fitting and why an amendment has been brought in. The explanatory notes are very brief, of course, but it would be of great assistance to
IMr. Fulton.]
us, as we have not had very long to study the matter, if the minister gave us a brief introduction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. I think clause 1 stands by itself. It is made necessary by the fact that last year we amended both the Yukon Act and the Northwest Territories Act in order to set up courts of appeal for those territories. Prior to that time it had been necessary for them to have recourse to the courts of appeal of certain of the provinces, but now they have a court of appeal in the territories. We are therefore changing the words here in order to provide that, in the Yukon Territory, it is "the court of appeal" instead of "the court of appeal for the province of British Columbia" and similarly with regard to the Northwest Territories.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 2-Service of Process.

I hesitate to be on my feet all the time, but it may be that in clause 2 the minister has done something which it was not the intention to do. I was just idly looking at subparagraph (a). In the case of a municipal corporation service will be made on the mayor, secretary-treasurer or clerk of the corporation. I am thinking of one municipality in my riding in which there is no mayor, no secretary-treasurer or no clerk. Therefore it would be impossible to effect service. I know that the minister is a big city boy and it may be that most of the people on the other side of the house are in that category. I am not sure about all the provinces, but in the province of Ontario we have municipalities which do not have as their head a mayor; they are reeves. There are many cases of municipalities which do not have a secretary-treasurer. They may have a secretary or a treasurer but they are not always a secretary-treasurer. In those cases there is often no clerk. In the one municipality, a village of which I was thinking, you would find there was a reeve, a secretary and a treasurer but none of the three offices which are indicated in subsection (a). I wondered whether it might be considered by the minister that this subsection should stand and that some consideration be given to the fact that there are municipalities other than cities whose heads are not mayors. In the Ontario municipal act the matter is covered by a reference to the head of the municipality, not the mayor or the reeve.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think I can only say that, far from being a big city person myself, I am a small town lawyer and proud of the fact. I am therefore prepared to admit that the hon. member has a point there the

answer to which I do not have at the moment. If there is a municipal corporation that has no mayor or secretary-treasurer or clerk,
I do not know what the answer would be. It may be that the Interpretation Act would provide us with an answer but we shall be glad to look into that matter. Perhaps in the meantime the clause might stand. I am afraid that we may have fallen into the error of taking it for granted that, because an almost identical provision appears twice elsewhere in the code, it had been tried and found not wanting. Perhaps it just has not been tried. Perhaps also the municipal corporations of these small places that my hon. friend has in mind would never be guilty of anything requiring service of process under the Criminal Code. I think that would be the most likely answer, Mr. Chairman.
That undoubtedly is the answer.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 2 stand?

Agreed.
Clause stands.
Clause 3 agreed to.
On clause 4-Order prohibiting driving.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I find that I did not have time to make the necessary study after the hon. member for Charlotte and the hon. member for Pictou raised a question regarding giving magistrates absolute jurisdiction to try the offence of driving a motor vehicle while disqualified.
In this bill we have provided that it shall be indictable, and by virtue of clause 18 within the absolute jurisdiction of the magistrate. It has not previously been indictable, but it will be indictable and absolute when this bill is passed. I have had my memory refreshed now and I am reminded that the reason why we thought this was appropriate was because it is a relatively simple issue; it is not a difficult legal issue. The issue is simple: has an order prohibiting driving been made, and was the accused driving the motor vehicle while under that prohibition?
It is not a difficult legal issue and therefore we thought it was one quite appropriate to leave in the hands of the magistrate, even though the penalty has been increased. The penalty has been increased for the reason referred to by several hon. members, namely that we think it is a serious matter and persons should be required to take seriously an order prohibiting them from driving.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
Criminal Code
On clause 5-Dangerous operation of vessel, etc.
Mr. Chairman, with regard to clause 5, suppose a child of 11 or 12 years of age is guilty of an offence under this clause, what would happen in that case? We are dealing here with the penal law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course, the case could be tried in juvenile court. I do not think the position here is any different from that of a child accused of another criminal offence.

I know of the case of a young boy of 10 years of age who was driving a motor boat on a lake-I think it was in the riding of Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm-a few years ago and four people were drowned. The father was arrested on a charge of manslaughter because of his negligence in performing his duty as father of the child. He was acquitted, by the way. In my remarks a few minutes ago I suggested to the minister that we should provide a minimum age for operating certain classes of boats. I wonder whether the minister has any comment to make on this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the position here is simply one of the general application of the provisions of the Criminal Code, which set the absolute age below which no person shall be charged with a criminal offence. As I recall, the age is seven years. In the case of an indictable offence by a child over 14 years of age it would be in the discretion of the juvenile court whether he should be prosecuted under the Criminal Code in the ordinary courts or whether the case should be proceeded with in the juvenile court. However, because the Juvenile Delinquents Act is not in force in all parts of Canada it would be quite inappropriate for us to say that children of a certain age must have their cases disposed of in juvenile court. We think we should merely create the offence and then leave it to the determination of the authorities in the ordinary way as to the method by which these cases are dealt with.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 6-Theft of telecommunication service.

Mr. Chairman, I should just like to ask the minister this interesting question; that is, interesting to me. In the first part of clause 6 the word "colour" is spelt c-o-l-o-u-r. Why is the Oxford dictionary spelling, which is the preferred spelling, used in the clause and the Funk and Wagnalls dictionary spelling, which is the United States spelling, used in the explanation? Does this

Criminal Code
represent a difference of opinion in the minister's department, or a concession to the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think it might be said to represent a very neat compromise. I could rationalize this by saying that in the code itself the spelling "o-u-r" is used throughout, but in the explanatory note- which is of course of no statutory value in so far as the bill itself is concerned-we have apparently used the spelling "o-r". We have at least saved one letter in the explanatory note.
Is it the practice of the department, in the spelling of words, to use the Oxford dictionary style of spelling?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, that is correct. The "color" in the explanatory note is a typographical error.
Thank you. I am very glad to hear that.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 7-Presumption from cheque issued without funds.
Mr. Chairman, would the minister give an explanation of the reasons for this amendment, or perhaps the representations which were made in connection with this proposed amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this arises primarily out of the fact that there was a case where a cheque was drawn on an institution that was not a bank and a conviction could not be obtained. Since caisses populaires, credit unions and other legitimate and worthy institutions which are not banks have increasingly entered into this field and to all intents and purposes have cheques drawn upon them, we thought this was an omission in the Criminal Code which should be rectified. The amendment is simply to add the words "or other institution".

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
Clause 8 agreed to.
On clause 9-False messages.

Mr. Chairman, would the minister tell the committee how it is proposed to convict anyone of this offence. What kind of evidence could be adduced in connection with threats made by telephone? I think it is an excellent provision, if you can make it work.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it might be difficult, but on the other hand I think it might be possible. Certainly in so far as a telegram is concerned it should be possible to establish that a certain person actually 
conveyed information in a telegram. In connection with the telephone, it is possible to obtain direct evidence that a telephone call came in at a certain time and a certain person actually placed that call at that time. I do not think it would be easy, but we certainly think the actions described here should be made an offence.
May I suggest it is more in the nature of an educative process; it is there, and that is supposed to deter people from doing it, even though it may be very difficult to prove?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have never been one to place too much store on the deterrent effect of criminal legislation. We had that discussion in connection with the capital punishment bill. However, if the course of action were persisted in, I think my hon. friend will appreciate that certain checks could be made that would establish the facts with reasonable certainty and might well support a prosecution.
Certainly in the casual or isolated call I doubt very much whether you could ever obtain the evidence, but if it were a course of conduct persisted in, I think it might well be possible to obtain the evidence.

Mr. Chairman, I said in my remarks a few minutes ago, and I think the hon. member for Kootenay West said the same thing, that clause 9 does not cover the most ordinary case of nuisance by telephone. The first and second parts of this clause provide:
(1)	Every one who, with intent to injure or alarm any person, conveys or causes or procures to be conveyed by letter, telegram, telephone, cable, radio, or otherwise, information-
(2)	Every one who, with intent to alarm or annoy any person, makes any indecent telephone call to such person is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.
These are not the ordinary cases. I think the most common case is simply annoyance by telephone

somebody would phone 25 times in a day and when they answered they would hang up the phone. It is not covered.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is true. I do not think the case of a person who places a call and hangs up as soon as he hears a telephone lifted at the other end is covered by this section. An attempt to deal with it here might possibly create an offence more embracing than was intended or desired. There might be a number of innocent explanations as to the reason for hanging up at the other end. It might be that on two or three occasions an innocent explanation would prevail. Perhaps a mother who was calling would have to hang up the telephone to go to a child who had fallen. We feel that the

section here has gone as far as is to be desired and that the danger of such a course as has been suggested would outweigh any possible advantages.

The minister and his
department might consider putting something similar into the nuisance section to make it an offence to annoy another person by telephone calls. This would not be such a serious offence and it would not be so difficult to prove.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We shall be glad to look at that suggestion if it is not covered already by the nuisance section, and see whether we can adopt it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 11-Saving provision.

I want to thank the minister for explaining what the penalty was. I did not realize it is as severe as it is. This is an increasing problem, especially in backwoods areas. People go hunting and pull up a stake or something of that sort, knowing they should not do it but not realizing the damage they are causing. I know of one case where it cost $1,500 to relocate a stake because they had to go back many miles to relocate timber limits by reference to other markers.
I wonder if it would be possible to have some small notices made available, or what other steps could be taken to give publicity to this matter. I know that is a provincial matter, but the minister's officials are in contact with the provincial attorneys general and it seems to me that this question might well receive some publicity even in local post offices because I am sure the majority of people do not realize how serious it is. It is impossible to find out who does these things when this damage is done miles from anywhere. I wonder if there is any way of bringing this to the attention of attorneys general.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sure this could be drawn to the attention of attorneys general and they might decide to give some publicity to it but that, of course, is something they themselves have to decide. Perhaps this discussion today and the reminder that the penalty is five years may go a long way to serving the purpose the hon. gentleman has in mind.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 12-Exception.
What is the exact purpose of this clause and also clause 13? Will the minister give us the background?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Clause 12 deals with the situation which arises when a person charged with
Criminal Code
an offence in one province wishes to plead guilty to an outstanding offence in another province. Clause 13 deals with the situation where an accused person charged with an offence in a province wishes to plead guilty to an outstanding charge against him elsewhere in the same province. The purpose of both clauses is to enable all the outstanding charges against an accused person to be disposed at one time so that he does not have to face a situation where, having served a sentence on one charge he is liable to be apprehended in the same or another province and prosecuted again.
At the present time in both cases the consent of the attorney general of the province concerned is necessary before an accused person can plead guilty to other charges. We have thought this should be preserved only in the case where a charge is outstanding in a different province. There the consent of the attorney general of that province will still be necessary before the charge can be disposed of. But where the outstanding charge is in the same province we feel the accused person should have the absolute right to have all the charges disposed of at the same time. We feel there is not the degree of administrative or other difficulty which would warrant anyone refusing to allow the accused to have the charges all to be disposed of at the same time when they arise in the same province. But where the outstanding charge is in another province we have retained the necessity for obtaining the consent of the attorney general of such province but we provide that it may be given by the deputy attorney general because it does not seem logical to insist that the attorney general must personally sign all these documents.

One of the phrases in the clause reads this way: "Where the accused is in custody". Does that mean in custody undergoing punishment or in custody waiting to be tried for an offence? Would it include waiting to be tried for an offence and being out on bail, even?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that the better view is that this would apply on either occasion, when a man is in custody pending the disposition of a charge or when he is in custody following conviction. I would remind the committee that the Fauteux commission made a recommendation on these lines and the change has also been asked for by the uniformity commissioners, who represent the attorneys general of the provinces.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Clause agreed to.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Criminal Code
On clause 14-By peace officer.

Would the minister say whether this provision will be of some assistance to us in the riding of Niagara Falls so that peace officers will be entitled to arrest without warrant anyone who throws himself into the upper Niagara river?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think that would be left to the discretion of the peace officer.
What is the reason for spelling out attempted suicide here? I thought that was covered by the former section.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under the Criminal Code, attempted suicide is only punishable on summary conviction, so a peace officer could not arrest without a warrant merely where he has reasonable and probable grounds to believe. In order to make it possible for these officers, who are confronted with a situation where a man is about to jump over a bridge, to arrest the individual, one has to make attempted suicide punishable as an indictable offence.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 14 carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sorry, but the change that has to be made is one that provides that a peace officer may arrest without a warrant, where he has reasonable and probable grounds to believe that a person is about to commit suicide.

speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
Clause 15 agreed to.
On clause 16.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The amendments to clauses 16 and 17, Mr. Chairman, are consequential upon the capital punishment bill that passed through the house a few weeks ago.

Clause agreed to.
Clauses 17 to 25 inclusive agreed to.
On clause 26.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in respect to clause 26, my hon. friends opposite asked if I could give the background. Clause 26 is the clause which arises out of the recommendation of the McRuer commission on the law of insanity.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
Clauses 27 to 31 inclusive agreed to.
On clause 32-Dangerous sexual offenders.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister what the purpose was of adding the words "or is likely to commit a further sexual offence," to the definition as recommended by the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This idea was suggested by the uniformity commissioners as being a further test available to the court on the basis of which it could reach a conclusion as to whether or not a person should be adjudged a dangerous sexual offender. I think the hon. lady will agree that this creates a second and alternative test as a basis on which to form a judgment, and we felt it was a proper proposal.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 33-Application for preventive detention.

Mr. Chairman, a portion of this clause reads as follows:
Where an accused has been convicted of an indictable offence the court may-
Whereas, section 661 reads in part:
Where an accused has been convicted-
When we consider section 662 we find that it provides that seven clear days' notice must be given to the accused before conviction, and then at page 13, paragraph (b) also provides that either before or after conviction notice may be served. I should like the minister to explain, regarding the service of notice, how an application can be made for an indeterminate detention before there is a conviction?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the answer to that question is that if the crown has in its possession, before the trial commences, evidence of the record of the accused in respect of other matters which, in the opinion of the crown, establish that the accused is an habitual criminal or a dangerous sexual offender then the crown can decide at that point to make application to have the individual so declared. Under those circumstances this amendment makes it clear that notice of this application may be given before or after conviction.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 34.

Mr. Chairman, again I wonder why the minister or his department have varied substantially from the terminology of the McRuer commission in its recommendation in regard to section 661 (3), which suggests that where the court finds an accused to be a dangerous sexual offender it shall, notwithstanding anything in this act or any other act of the parliament of Canada, sentence the accused to preventive detention; whereas the bill before us suggests that the sentence of preventive detention shall be in lieu of any other sentence that might be imposed, or in addition to any sentence that

was imposed if that sentence had expired. Why is it necessary to add those words?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The answer to that is that we have included here the additional principle of providing that the crown may make application subsequent to conviction and sentence. We felt, in conformity with the intent of the McRuer commission's recommendation, that after the accused had been sentenced to a determinate period and the application was granted, then the court should impose an indeterminate sentence in lieu of the determinate sentence that had already been imposed. I think this carries out the intent of the McRuer recommendation, varying only because of the circumstances which we now are including, and which were not contemplated by the McRuer commission.

Mr. Chairman, there is a principle of law that once a trier has heard a case and has come to a conclusion he is functus. In this case, where the judge has tried the matter, has convicted and imposed a short term of sentence, following which an application is made, within the three-month period, to another judge to have the individual declared a dangerous sexual offender, the other judge may sentence the individual to an indeterminate period in lieu of the first sentence. In other words, the second judge, who has not been seized with the case at all, has the rights of an appeal court and can wipe out the determinate sentence and substitute an indeterminate sentence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think there is anything contained here beyond the principle that a court of appeal may vary a sentence. All we are doing in principle is allowing a change in the sentence and providing by statute that, where a person is adjudged to be a dangerous sexual offender, the court that makes that finding shall impose an indeterminate sentence. The statute then says that the sentence is in lieu of the determinate sentence which may already have been imposed. I think this principle carries out the intention of the McRuer commission report.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PURCHASE AND SALE OF SECURITIES BY MINISTER, ETC.
speechtext:
Basically that is the purpose, so that in the case of an assignment of a crown debt the individual will be in the same position as though there had been an assignment of an ordinary debt by a subject and, as will appear later in the following subsection, an assignment of a chose in action.
As I endeavoured to outline at the resolution stage, when the house was in the committee of the whole, the position which has traditionally been taken by the crown in the past is that the crown is not bound by an assignment of a debt owing by the crown to a subject. Over the years there has been developed a practice whereby the banks, and indeed other persons engaged in the business, have accepted from crown creditors powers of attorney. They arranged their affairs, in many cases, apparently on the basis that such powers of attorney operated essentially in the same way as assignments, although in fact they did not confer on the donee any rights, as against the crown, to be paid in place of the crown creditor at the resolution stage. I outlined the particular case in the exchequer court of the Bank of Nova Scotia in respect to an assignment made by Roy Swail Limited. This case was heard by the president of the exchequer court who decided that the crown was in the same position with respect to the assignment of a debt owing to it as was any subject, provided that the assignment was made in accordance with the laws of assignment of the province in which the assignment was made, and that adequate notice of such assignment was given to the crown.
The purpose of these amendments, which are encompassed by new section 88 with the various letters, is to provide a simple and adequate procedure for the subject so that it is possible to have an assignment proceed, as the president of the exchequer court did decide, and that there may be no prejudice either to the subject or to the crown. The effect of the amendment is to provide for the recognition of the assignment of crown debts arising under contract, but subject to certain rights and conditions which we will discuss later.
It is also proposed to include, as I indicated earlier, provisions whereby the governor in council may authorize the recognition and assignment of other choses in action, subject to the same rules and conditions.

speakeroldname: Mr. Richard A. Bell (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill, together with its companion bill which follows immediately and deals with loan companies, parallels in large measure the amendments already made this session to the insurance acts, the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act and the Foreign Insurance Companies Act. This bill revises and modernizes the powers of federally incorporated trust companies. I am in the hands of the house, sir, whether the bill should be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce for further study or should proceed to the committee of the whole. Whatever the procedure may be, the house might wish to have a little background information about trust companies generally.
There are just over 50 trust companies operating in Canada at the present time. Ten were incorporated by or under the authority of this parliament and the remainder were incorporated provincially. Looking at the field of trust companies as a whole, the ten federally incorporated companies transact between one fifth and one quarter of the total business of all trust companies in Canada. These ten companies, whose names I shall mention, have capital and reserve funds approximating $40 million and administer trust funds totalling about $1,500 million.
The federally incorporated companies are these, and I will give after each the year of incorporation:
Year of
Name	Incorporation
The Canada Permanent Trust Company 1913
The Canada Trust Company	 1894
Chartered Trust Company	 1905
Commercial Trust Company Limited ..	1904
The Eastern Trust Company	 1893
Guaranty Trust Company of Canada ..	1925
Investors Trust Company	 1957
The Premier Trust Company	 1913
Prudential Trust Company Limited ..	1909
The Sterling Trusts Corporation	 1911
Originally, sir, the Trust Companies Act in Canada was enacted in 1914 and it applies to all federally incorporated trust companies but of course has no application to provincially incorporated companies. Consequently, the amendments to the act now proposed by Bill No. S-28 would apply only to the ten companies which I have mentioned and which are federally incorporated.

But not to a trust company which has been incorporated and is not now functioning, like the Standard Trust Company which was given a charter two years ago. I do not believe it is in operation. The amendments would not apply to that company?
Trust Companies Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My recollection does not extend, as the hon. gentleman's does, to the Standard Trust Company. This bill would apply to all trust companies federally incorporated.
To all?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: To all.
Not only to the ten; that is the point.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
If there are others not within my knowledge at the present time, then this bill would have such application.
Since 1914, the federally incorporated companies have been required to file financial statements annually with the Minister of Finance, but there was no provision for licensing or regular inspection or supervision until 1920. Since that year, federal trust companies have been required to operate under a licence from the minister of finance and under the provisions of the department of insurance, under its distinguished deputy head, Mr. Kenneth R. MacGregor.
The investment and lending powers of federal trust companies are specified, as I have indicated, in the Trust Companies Act. It has been the custom of parliament to keep these powers consistent with the corresponding powers of insurance companies, except in so far as differences may be necessary by reason of the special characteristics of trust companies. In view of the amendments recently made to the insurance act, it is now proposed to make similar amendments to the investment and lending powers of trust companies to the extent deemed appropriate. In addition, a few other amendments are proposed, either for clarification or to enable the companies to meet changing conditions. With respect to those, I shall deal in some detail.
Perhaps for clarification of my subsequent remarks, it might be mentioned that the assets of trust companies are divided into three categories as follows:	First, unguaranteed trust funds. These are the funds accepted by the company in trust to be administered in accordance with the terms of the trust but carrying no guarantee of security of principal or of interest yield. Then, second, there are the guaranteed trust funds, those funds accepted by the company in trust where the company guarantees the security of the principal and sometimes the interest yield. They consist mainly of deposits made by the public in individual deposit accounts and of funds realized from the sale of guaranteed investment certificates. Third, and finally, there are the company funds. These are funds

Trust Companies Act
owned by the shareholders themselves, and they consist principally of the capital, surplus and reserves of the company.
The Trust Companies Act deals separately with the investment and lending powers applicable to each category. Such powers relating to trust funds are found in section 64 and those relating to company funds are found in section 68 to which reference is made in Bill No. S-28.
I should like to outline the more important and detailed amendments proposed in respect of investments and loans, all of such amendments relating to trust funds being found in clause 1 of the bill and those relating to the company's own funds being found in clause 2.
First, may I deal with the limits on mortgage loans. Hon. members are familiar with this situation in view of what transpired recently in connection with insurance companies. At present, companies may invest in and lend on the security of mortgages on real estate but the amount so invested or loaned in any particular case must not exceed 60 per cent of the value of the real estate. What is proposed by this bill is to raise this limit from 60 per cent to 66| per cent. This change would apply to all three categories of funds which I have mentioned and is parallel to the change recently made in respect of insurance companies.
Hon. gentlemen, as they review the bill, may see what appears to be duplication or repetition in the bill. This is attributable to the separate identification of investment powers and lending powers and also to the three separate categories in which the funds of trust companies are divided.
Then, may I outline the second category, real estate for the production of income. Companies may now invest a limited amount of guaranteed trust funds and company funds in real estate for the production of income, either alone or jointly with any other federal trust company or loan company, where the real estate is leased to a corporation having a dividend record meeting the prescribed standard of the act. The maximum amount that may be so invested in any one parcel of real estate is one half of 1 per cent of the aggregate of the book value of the guaranteed trust funds and the company's own funds. It is proposed to raise this limit from one half of 1 per cent to 1 per cent. It is proposed also to permit a company to join with any trust company, loan company or insurance company incorporated in Canada in making such investments. These changes are parallel to changes recently made for insurance companies.
Hon. gentlemen who sat in the banking and commerce committee when considering the insurance bills will remember the discussion

there which related to equipment trust certificates. There is a similar provision in this bill. Companies may now invest guaranteed trust funds and company funds in equipment trust certificates issued for the purchase of railway transportation equipment. It is proposed, under this bill, to expand this class to include transportation equipment for use on public highways. As I have said, this parallels a change which was made in respect of insurance companies.
Then, fourth, I would deal with investments and loans which are not specifically authorized under the act. It is proposed that companies be permitted, with respect to company funds only, to make investments and loans not otherwise authorized by the act, subject to a maximum limit on the amount of funds that may be so applied. This would grant to such companies a rather small area of freedom of investment of their own funds similar to that which is now available to insurance companies. The proposed limit on the amount that may be so invested and loaned is 15 per cent of the company's unimpaired paid up capital and reserve. This limit is the same as is prescribed in the loan and trust corporations act of Ontario in similar circumstances, and there are advantages in having the same limit apply to federally incorporated companies.
For a company having the maximum capital and reserve permitted by the act in relation to its guaranteed trust funds, this limit would represent a little over 1 per cent of all the company funds and guaranteed trust funds. This may be compared with a limit of 5 per cent of the assets now permitted for insurance companies. Hon. members may wonder why the difference between 5 per cent for insurance companies and 1 per cent for trust companies. The lower limit for trust companies is considered appropriate, at least until some experience develops with the use of this area of freedom of investment. It is not proposed that such area of freedom would extend in any way the company's power to invest in mortgages or hypothecs on real estate, to invest in real estate or to lend on the security of real estate.
In what clause of the bill is that covered?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I believe the particular provision is contained in clause 2, subclause 4.
Then I deal with the limit on investment in common stock. Companies may now invest guaranteed trust funds and company funds in preferred stocks or common stocks of Canadian corporations where the dividend record of the issuing corporation meets a specified

standard set in the act. As respects guaranteed trust funds, not more than 15 per cent of the book value may be invested in common stocks and not more than 25 per cent may be invested in, or loaned on the security of, stocks of all kinds, whether common or preferred. As respects company funds, not more than 15 per cent of the book value may be invested in common stocks and the total invested in, or loaned on the security of, stocks of all kinds, whether common or preferred, may not exceed 25 per cent of the company's unimpaired paid up capital and reserve.
The companies have requested an increase in the existing limits on investments in common stocks. Since at the present time, companies have virtually none of their guaranteed trust funds invested in stocks, it is not proposed to raise the limit applicable to those funds. As respects company funds, however, several companies are near the limit and it is proposed to remove the 15 per cent limit on common stocks in that connection but to retain the limit of 25 per cent of unimpaired paid up capital and reserve as the limit on investments in and loans on the security of stocks of all kinds. So in order to maintain consistency with the insurance companies and the loan companies, it is proposed that the amount of the company's own funds invested in common stocks when added to the amount of guaranteed trust funds invested in common stocks shall not exceed 15 per cent of the total of such funds. The effect of this change would be to permit an increase in investments in common stocks with respect to company funds where a company has not used its full powers in guaranteed trust funds and provided that less than 10 per cent of company funds have been invested in preferred stocks.
This is a detailing of the significant changes which are in themselves rather detailed and complex in so far as they affect the investment and lending powers of the companies.
I should like to take just a moment or two in which to deal with two other matters. First, I should like to deal with the power of a federally incorporated trust company to purchase the assets and business of another trust company, whether the latter be a federally incorporated or a provincially incorporated company. Certain of the proposed amendments in this respect are to be found in clause 3 of the bill.
The act at present permits a company to buy 67 per cent or more of the stock of another trust company, subject to approval by the treasury board, where the purchase is made as a prelude to the eventual taking over of the assets and business of the purchased company. The act specifies that at least 67 90205-6-415
Trust Companies Act
per cent of the stock of the company to be taken over must be purchased at the outset but it does not clearly specify that in any offer to purchase, the same offer must be extended to all shareholders of the company being purchased. It is proposed to include such a requirement in section 79 in order to prevent discrimination against minority shareholders.
Another amendment to this section would authorize the purchasing company to have a larger board of directors, temporarily, following acquisition of the stock of the other company, than is ordinarily permitted by section 15 which places the maximum number at 30. The temporarily enlarged board could not, however, in any case exceed the aggregate number of directors of both companies at the time of purchase. This amendment is for the purpose of enabling the directors of the other company to become directors of the purchasing company, thus retaining the value of their goodwill, service and connections for the benefit of the purchasing company.
I said earlier there were two things which I wanted to mention. I should have said three. The third and final is the fact that it is considered desirable to include in the act provisions whereby federal trust companies might amalgamate as an alternative to merging by the purchase and sale of assets and business. Federal trust companies have had the power to merge by the purchase and sale of assets and business ever since the Trust Companies Act was enacted in 1914 but they do not at present possess the power to achieve the same end by amalgamation, notwithstanding the advantages of the latter course in some circumstances. For many years the chartered banks similarly enjoyed the power to merge by purchase and sale but they lacked the power to amalgamate until granted such power on revision of the Bank Act in 1954. Canadian insurance companies, on the other hand, have possessed the power to follow this course since 1910. Many provincially incorporated trust companies likewise have had the power for many years to amalgamate under the applicable provincial statutes, thus leaving federally incorporated trust companies at a disadvantage in this respect. Hon. gentlemen will observe that clause 4 of the bill, which would enact a new section 80A, has been designed at the request of federal trust companies to fill this gap and put them in the same position as most other kinds of companies. It might be noted that this clause makes provision for the amalgamation of one federally incorporated trust company with another federally incorporated trust company but makes no provision for the

Trust Companies Act
amalgamation of a federally incorporated trust company with a provincially incorporated trust company or with any other kind of company.
We have no power.

The main purpose of this bill is to make certain changes in the investment powers of trust companies incorporated by parliament.

We find that this bill will enable a company to invest its own funds in mortgages on real estate up to a maximum of two thirds of the value of the real estate instead of 60 per cent. Mr. Chairman, as this legislation has been in existence for some time it would seem that it has a very good purpose in that the crown in the right of the Dominion of Canada owns large tracts of land. Many areas come to mind such as that at Petawawa. People have occasions to travel over portions of the property there every day and therefore there must be a way of enforcing traffic laws similar to those contained in the traffic acts of the various provinces. I have not had occasion to read the numerous sections of the regulations which, if the volume that the minister held in his hand a moment ago is any indication, are rather numerous, but it seems to me that reference should be made to the travelled portions of these lands if the regulations pertain to traffic. In other words, these provisions would make very little sense if the crimes could be punishable when committed on other than a highway. Under most provincial highway acts, if the same crime were committed in a private driveway or on a person's farm, a person could not be convicted. No doubt the intention of this legislation is to make sure that the same exemption is preserved in so far as these large tracts of land are concerned which the crown owns.
If this bill relates to traffic offences, it seems to me the wording should be such as to limit the offence to the travelled portion of the property. If a person drove negligently on a portion of government property other than the travelled portion and thereby caused damage to another vehicle, there could be confusion as to the laying of a charge. The amending bill before us indicates that most of the provincial highways traffic acts impose

If it is the intention of this amending bill to bring the penalties into line with the penalties imposed by provincial highway traffic acts, it seems to me that it fails because a person may commit a very grave offence while visiting government property for the first and last time, and therefore the judge has no power beyond depriving him of his right to drive on that portion of federal property. Because this is the last opportunity I should like to ask the Minister of Veterans Affairs if consideration has been given to a certain matter and if by any chance the hon. gentleman contemplates any amendment of this act to give recognition to a forgotten group of people. I refer to the merchant seamen who were in the front line of war. Thousands of Canadians died on merchant ships in the front line. They have never been recognized by any public act in Canada. I should like to ask the minister, taking advantage of this discussion on clause 1, which is the only opportunity I have, whether consideration is being given in this measure or any other to those who survived as far as recognition by Canada in the matter of pensions is concerned.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF ALLOWANCES AND INCOME CEILINGS, ETC.
speechtext:
I had no opportunity of taking part in the discussion which took place on the resolution stage of this bill to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act and at this time I do not want to delay the bill. However, as a disabled veteran of the first world war and one who has been in close contact with some of these veterans from the first world war I feel sure this amendment will be of great benefit to the recipients who in many cases have served in both wars.
I am pleased, on looking over the bill, to see some of the changes which are to be made, especially the addition of time taken to travel to England and back again-in my case, 14 days going over and 10 days coming back. In some cases this extension will enable a number of veterans to qualify. I should like to commend the minister and the government on bringing in this fine legislation.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF ALLOWANCES AND INCOME CEILINGS, ETC.
speechtext: I do not often commend the government but I should like to do so on this occasion. I think this is a very good bill. I welcome it on behalf of many people in my constituency who will benefit from it. I think it is timely and worth while, and I should like to thank the government for introducing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF ALLOWANCES AND INCOME CEILINGS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to answer the hon. member for Vancouver East who raised a question concerning merchant seamen. I have given consideration to this problem affecting merchant seamen. It was one of the


first questions I raised with my departmental officials when I assumed this porfolio last fall.
Along with others, I have a great deal of admiration for merchant seamen who served in many instances in such perilous conditions during war time. I admit, frankly, that had I been asked to perform some of the duties undertaken by merchant seamen I might have been somewhat reluctant to come forward quickly.
A question with regard to merchant seamen was raised in the standing committee on veterans affairs, and my parliamentary secretary answered the question there. It amounts to this-that although there is a difficulty in bringing merchant seamen under the provisions of the War Veterans Allowance Act as it stands now because of the requirements set out in the act we think, nevertheless, that merchant seamen might be dealt with more properly under the civilian war pensions and allowances act. We are giving consideration to this problem. If this could be done it would obviate the necessity of declaring merchant seamen to be veterans under the definition which appears in the War Veterans Allowance Act. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East and with others who have raised this question that the problem has to be tackled and dealt with. I do not at all disguise my sympathy for the merchant seamen who are not at the present time benefiting under the War Veterans Allowance Act. Let us not forget, however, that those who were disabled have been taken care of.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF ALLOWANCES AND INCOME CEILINGS, ETC.
speechtext: I had not intended to intervene in this debate-

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF ALLOWANCES AND INCOME CEILINGS, ETC.
speechtext: The old, old story.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF ALLOWANCES AND INCOME CEILINGS, ETC.
speechtext:
-because we are anxious to get this legislation through and the hour is getting late, but what the minister has just said has caused me to rise and make a few remarks at this point.
I am grateful to the minister for telling the committee that this matter is under consideration but I would urge him to give consideration to bringing the merchant seamen under the War Veterans Allowance Act rather than under the civilian war pensions and allowances act as he has just suggested, because whatever act you bring these seamen under you will have to grapple with the problem of service and one of the big problems of the merchant navy is that there are so many different groups with so many different kinds of service-service on inland waters, service on coastal waters and service on the high seas. I do not think all of them can qualify, but I want to point out that this particular act which we are considering now, the War

Veterans Allowance Act, was set up for just such cases as these-for people who rendered service to their country in time of need and who are not qualified to receive regular service pensions. They were not wounded, they were not disabled, and perhaps there was some question as to whether they could be classed as veterans. I think this is where we should change our thinking. It is not enough to say that a person is a veteran because he served in a certain way. That, I think, is wrong thinking. Any man is a veteran who volunteered his services to his country in time of war and who risked his life in the service of his country. I will point out that the casualties in the merchant marine were often higher than in the regular service. A man can do no more than give his life. Of those who were spared I have many in my own district who are crippled with arthritis because of the soaking in the water that they underwent for hours, sometimes for days. I have others who are crippled with tuberculosis because they were cramped up in small quarters aboard ships. I have others who are crippled for other reasons traceable to their service in wartime. This act was set up to deal with such cases. If we call these people civilians we are throwing away the value of their service. We are saying to them that because they served in the merchant navy or because they were getting a certain rate of pay they are not veterans. I do not think that has anything to do with the definition of a veteran. A veteran is an individual who serves his country voluntarily in time of need. Surely these people are just as worthy and deserving of benefits under this act as those individuals in the other categories we have brought in.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF ALLOWANCES AND INCOME CEILINGS, ETC.
speechtext: Nobody is arguing with you.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF ALLOWANCES AND INCOME CEILINGS, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, yes they are. The minister suggested we had to keep away from thinking about bringing these individuals under the War Veterans Allowance Act, not considering them as veterans but as civilians.

speechtext: And he is right.

I do not think he is right. A veteran is not a veteran because he puts on a uniform. Many veterans are drawing benefits under this act who never saw service or took any risk. Why should we decide just because they wore a uniform, they are any more worthy, and should receive the benefits of this legislation, than those individuals who served in the merchant marine? I should like to urge the minister to cast off this kind of thinking and to devise some means of bringing these individuals under the terms of this legislation, which has been set up to look
War Veterans Allowance Act after those individuals who cannot qualify for a pension in any other way.

Mr. Chairman, unfortunately I am supposed to attend three committee meetings tomorrow morning and felt that this perhaps was my only chance to say very briefly what I wish to say in regard to this legislation.
I should like to know why we must continue this discrimination in respect to the 365 day provisions, and why we cannot just do away with it altogether. I suggest this is an attempt to keep alive some old sores from the first world war which ought to be forgotten. This measure should be abolished altogether so that those individuals who went overseas during the first world war will be treated in the same way as those individuals who went overseas during the second world war. I think it is very unfortunate that this is not what is being done at the present time.
I should also like to suggest, as has been suggested by other hon. members on this side of the house from Newfoundland, that the Newfoundland forestry corps should be treated as veterans on exactly the same basis as the Canadian forestry corps because, if Newfoundland had been in confederation at that time, they would be treated in that way. I should like to repeat that this is perhaps something which ought to have been done


in our day and was not, which is no excuse for the present government not doing it.
We all know that under the Canadian Citizenship Act every Newfoundlander is treated as a born Canadian. The members of the Newfoundland forestry corps should be treated with equality on the same basis as other veterans. These individuals performed exactly the same services but, because they were enlisted in a civilian corps, they are treated differently. I suggest that distinction should not be perpetuated and that there is still a chance during this committee's consideration for the minister to eliminate this distinction.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo put a motion on the order paper which, if I remember correctly, was passed, but I do not believe a return has been made yet, asking for a list of all those awards which have been made to a certain category of Newfoundland veteran. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Ottawa,
June 16, 1961.
The Honourable Leslie M. Frost, Q.C.,

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Premier of Ontario,
Toronto, Ontario.
My dear Premier:
At the dominion-provincial conference of February 23 and 24, 1961, I presented certain proposals with respect to the financial arrangements which might exist between Canada and the provinces for the five-year period commencing April 1, 1962. The major aspects of these proposals were that we should discontinue the present system of tax rentals in favour of tax collection arrangements, that the federal government would leave considerably more tax room for the provinces by withdrawing substantially in the personal income tax and that a broader system of equalization should be adopted which would give greater weight to fiscal need particularly when considered in conjunction with the proposal to increase substantially the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants and to continue for a further five years the special payment of $8 million per annum to Newfoundland.
The above proposals were discussed at the dominion-provincial conference of February 23-24. Since that time they have been discussed intensively by officials at two meetings of the continuing committee on fiscal and economic matters. The federal government has given very careful consideration to all the points raised and the purpose of my letter is to acquaint you with the conclusions we have reached.
In changing from a tax rental to a tax collection system of agreements, the first question to settle is the type of tax collection agreements which can be adopted to put the new system into effect. Under the system proposed the provinces will levy their own personal income and corporation income taxes. The Department of Justice has given intensive consideration to the possibility of devising agreements which would enable the Department of National Revenue to provide the tax collection service for those provinces which wished it without having to resort to provincial courts. If this could have been achieved, it would have greatly simplified the
task of the Department of National Revenue. However, it is the opinion of the Department of Justice that any arrangement which attempted to provide for the enforcement of the provincial taxes otherwise than through the provincial courts would be of doubtful constitutional validity. This means that the only type of tax collection agreement which can be safely entered into between the provinces and Canada is one in which the federal government will act as the agent of the province for the purpose of collecting the tax imposed by the province. The fact that an agency system of agreements must be entered into will complicate the work of the Department of National Revenue and will make it necessary to exercise extreme care in defining the relationship between the federal and provincial taxes.
A second important question has been raised involving the relationship between the federal and provincial taxes on personal income. Two possibilities have been discussed. The first is that the provincial tax might be a percentage of the federal tax. The second is that the provincial tax might be imposed on the basis of taxable income as defined under the Income Tax Act of Canada with a schedule of rates which followed the rate of progression in the federal income tax. The federal government is not prepared to offer tax collection agreements on both of these bases concurrently, partly because of the administrative complexity which would result for the Department of National Revenue, and partly because of the inconvenience it would cause to taxpayers and to employers who are responsible for tax deductions at source. In order that it will be possible to separate the provincial content of all tax deductions at source without installing a complete system of separate accounting for the provincial and federal levies, it is necessary that the percentage relationship between the provincial tax deductions and the federal tax deductions must be constant throughout the year. Since this is the case, it seems to the federal government that a provincial tax levied as a percentage of the federal tax has very clear advantages. We are prepared, therefore, to offer tax collection agreements to provinces in which the personal income tax is levied as a percentage of the federal tax.

There are no similar complications in the case of the corporation income tax and the federal government is prepared, therefore, to enter into tax collection agreements with the provinces for any corporation income tax which is expressed as a flat percentage of taxable income as defined for federal income tax purposes.
Some provinces have enquired as to the possibility of the federal government collecting for the provinces in addition to the income tax, a further flat rate tax which would apply subject to a stated dollar maximum as is the case with the federal old age security tax. The difficulty with this proposal is that the addition of such a tax to the provincial rate structure would destroy the uniform percentage relationship between the provincial and federal tax in all income ranges. The federal government could not, therefore undertake to collect such a special tax without becoming involved in completely separate accounting on an individual basis for the provincial and federal tax. This is a task which the federal government cannot assume because of the unnecessary additional burden it would place on the Department of National Revenue.
Questions have been raised as to whether natural resource revenue should be included in the formula and particularly whether certain elements of that natural resource revenue which have been referred to as non-recurring should be included. As I stated to the dominion provincial conference of February 23-24 in presenting the federal proposals, the reason for including natural resource revenue was to broaden the equalization formula by taking account of the great variation in provincial revenues due to natural resources. In our view, this addition to the equalization formula has greatly improved it from the standpoint of meeting the fiscal need of the provinces. The decision to include 50 per cent of all natural resource revenue as shown in the dominion bureau of statistics publication, "Financial Statistics of Provincial Governments", was taken to avoid uncertainty in the application of the formula. We believe that a thin line separates recurring from non-recurring revenues in the resource field, if indeed there is any line of separation at all. Consequently, to attempt any such separation would, we believe, lay the whole formula open to doubt and dispute. Since we are including only 50 per cent of natural resource revenue, we are not in any event allowing the full weight of either the recurring or non-recurring natural resource revenue to affect the equalization payments. I conclude, therefore, that the proposal to include 50 per cent of natural resource revenue in the equalization formula should stand as an essential part of the federal offer.
Some provinces have asked whether the federal government would be prepared to extend the guarantees offered under the federal proposals. One suggestion was that there should be an additional guarantee that no province would receive less in equalization under the new proposals than it would have received under a projection of the equalization component of the present arrangements. Another suggestion was that what was referred to in my statement to the conference as the (a) guarantee should be extended to provinces above the national average. Under the proposals as presented by the federal government, the provinces will receive the benefit of substantially increased tax room in addition to equalization and the equalization guarantees. The federal withdrawal from the personal income tax is to be raised to 20 per cent by the end of the period compared with the standard rate of 13 per cent for the present year. Having in mind its heavy responsibilities, the federal government cannot provide additional equalization guarantees of the type mentioned above while at the same time offering substantially increased tax room to the provinces.
A further question was raised with respect to the application of the equalization guarantee to those provinces in receipt of the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants. The Atlantic provinces adjustment grants, which it is proposed to increase by $10 million, will be paid separately under the terms of the new legislation. However, in determining the additional equalization to be paid to a province in the form of a guarantee, it is proposed to take account of the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants. This seems a reasonable procedure in view of the fact that the guaranteed equalization already provides for payments to the provinces in excess of their entitlement under the basic equalization formula.
At the conference I stated that the federal government was prepared to consider certain concessions in connection with the taxation of the forest industry if the provinces were willing also to make some concessions. It has been conceded that because the logging profits tax is levied in addition to the corporation income tax, the forest industry bears a greater tax burden than other industries. The possibilities of lessening the burden of taxation on the forest industry have been discussed at the official level. One of the possibilities discussed was that a tax credit shared between a province and Canada, might be granted to the industry. Before this

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
can be done some further technical discussions will be required to reach agreement on the definition of logging income which will be subject to tax and accepted for the purpose of this tax credit. Subject to reaching agreement on this matter of the definition of logging income, the federal government is prepared as a means of relieving the tax burden on the forest industry to offer a tax credit equal to two thirds of the logging tax up to a maximum rate of 10 per cent, provided the province gives a tax credit equal to the remaining one third of such logging tax.
Request has been made for the preparation of a list of federal agencies and corporations which might be subject to provincial sales taxes. We are proceeding with the preparation of such a list and this matter will be resolved before the expiry of the present agreements at March 31st next.
I indicated in my statement to the conference of February 23-24, that the federal government was prepared to continue for the fiscal year 1961-62 the arrangements whereby the provinces receive a half share of the income tax collected from certain public utilities. A number of provinces have indicated that they believe there are strong reasons for continuing this sharing beyond the year 1961-62. We now propose as a concession to these representations to give the assurance that this sharing will be continued throughout the period of the next agreements,
that is, for the next five years up to and including the fiscal year 1966-67.
With regard to the progress which is being made with the preparation of legislation to implement the proposed financial arrangements for the period after March 31, 1962, it is our intention to introduce at the current session of parliament legislation which will provide the basis for the proposed new arrangements. The Department of Justice is making good progress with the drafting of this legislation. While the legislation will provide authority for the government of Canada to enter into tax collection agreements with the provinces, there will be a great deal of work involved in drafting the agreements themselves. This can come at a later stage. As soon as the draft legislation has been prepared which will provide the basis of the new arrangements, it will be possible for the Department of Justice to turn their attention to the preparation of model provincial legislation which would complement the draft federal legislation. I understand that it was the wish of some of the provinces that the federal government should assist them in this fashion.
I believe that the above comments deal with the major points which have been raised in connection with the federal proposals and I trust that they give you an adequate account of the progress to date.
I am,
Yours sincerely, John G. Diefenbaker.

speechtext: Tuesday, June 20, 1961
